The lesson for your own audit: list your last 30 posts, compute views ÷ subscribers for each, and find your own floor. Formats that live under the floor for three consecutive runs are paying for the channel's average, not adding to it.

The format mix: five load-bearing formats

Stripping the month to its skeletons, the channel runs five formats in rotation: the daily utility (the one post the niche opens the channel for), the teardown/analysis (the high-effort piece that earns forwards and defines the brand), the community prompt (a poll or question — the comments under these posts are the liveliest), the digest (weekly, structured, the most-saved post type), and the commercial slot (visible, labeled, capped at about one per ten posts). Notice what's absent: no clip-art motivation posts, no engagement-bait, no cross-posted filler. Every format either builds the daily-open habit, earns distribution, or pays the bills — and the mix is roughly 60/25/15 between them.

The monetization spacing: trust as inventory

Count the promo posts in the month: three. Each is a dedicated, labeled post with the sponsor's artifact attached (a checklist, a trial, a calculator) rather than a naked link — and each holds its views within 10% of the channel's non-promo average, which is the metric advertisers actually screen for. That's the compounding asset: sponsors pay for the audience's habit of not muting during ads, and the channel protects that habit by capping frequency and insisting on rewrites in its own voice. Compare with the decayed channel that runs daily promos: same subscriber line, ERR halved, ad rates lower. The spacing isn't modesty — it's pricing power maintained over years.

The operations: what the outside never sees

Three systems make the visible month possible. The capture pipeline: the channel's daily material comes from a source stack (feeds, a review chat, reader submissions) that feeds a queue days deep — the queue is why the rhythm never breaks. The analytics ritual: the format retirements and the floor maintenance above happen because someone checks ERR weekly; the calendar changes you can see in hindsight are decisions someone made on a Tuesday. The moderation stack: the linked discussion group runs captcha-on-join, a three-strike warn ladder and slow mode during launches — which is why the comment sections stay valuable enough to be part of the product. None of this appears in the public page; all of it shows up in the numbers.

Run the same teardown on your channel

The audit takes an hour and pays for months. 1) Scroll your own last 60 posts on the web preview and timestamp-map the week: are there dead days, bursts, dead hours? 2) Compute views ÷ subscribers for the last 30 and mark your floor — which formats live under it? 3) Name your five load-bearing formats; if you can't, the channel is publishing from moods, and the fix is the pillar system. 4) Count promos and check whether they hold views relative to your average — that ratio is your ad inventory's real price. 5) Open your discussion group as a stranger: would you comment there? Every gap this audit finds is fixable within a quarter — the teardown is less about copying a big channel and more about discovering which of its systems yours is missing.

faq.q: How do I find channels worth studying for a teardown like this?
faq.a: Use TGStat or Telemetr catalogs filtered to your niche and size band, and pick channels whose ERR looks anomalously good for their size — that anomaly is usually an operating system worth reading. Then open the public web preview (t.me/s/channelname) and scroll a full month. You are looking for rhythm, format discipline and how promo posts perform relative to the average — all visible from the outside.

faq.q: How many promotional posts per month is sustainable?
faq.a: The pattern among channels that hold their ERR while monetizing is roughly one promo per eight to twelve posts — for a daily channel, two to four dedicated promos a month. The number matters less than the ratio staying constant: channels that let promos creep upward watch ERR slide over the following quarter and end up selling their ads at the lower rate their own dilution created.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to spot a badly run channel from the outside?
faq.a: Three tells: irregular timestamps (dead days followed by multi-post bursts), a wide view band (some posts at triple the channel norm, some at a tenth — no floor, no quality gate), and promo posts that hold far fewer views than the average, which means the audience has learned to skip them. All three are visible on the public web preview without any tools.

faq.q: My channel is small — does this teardown logic still apply?
faq.a: The systems shrink but do not change. A 500-subscriber channel benefits from the same five-format rotation, the same weekly ERR glance and the same promo spacing, because these are habits that scale; retrofitting them at 40,000 subscribers is much harder than installing them at 500. The one difference: at small size, err on the side of more community formats, since early channels live on their comment sections.

telegram-community-management.title: Managing a Telegram Community: The Owner’s Playbook for the First Year
telegram-community-management.desc: Running a Telegram community that survives growth: culture-setting in the first 90 days, moderation ladders, conflict triage, rituals that retain, and the systems that keep it from consuming you.
telegram-community-management.content:
A Telegram channel is a broadcast; a Telegram community is a living thing — and the difference is the discussion group, where the audience talks back. Communities compound (members recruit members, culture self-moderates, the group becomes the product) and they collapse (the founder becomes the bottleneck, the spam wave wins, the conversation curdles). The difference between the two outcomes is rarely luck — it's a handful of systems installed early. This is the playbook for the first year, in the order the systems are needed.

The first 90 days: setting the culture on purpose

Culture is easiest to set when everyone can see everyone. Days 1–30: the seeding window. Personally welcome every joiner by name (at this size you can), answer every question within hours, and be publicly generous to the first regulars — the people who watch you treat the first ten members well are deciding how to treat the next hundred. Days 31–60: the standards window. Pin the two artifacts that do twenty jobs: a rules post (five rules maximum — more is a sign nothing is enforced) and a "what this group is for" post with one concrete example of a great exchange. Days 61–90: the delegation window. Promote your first moderator from the members who already do the work unasked — the person who answers newbies, not the loudest commenter. A moderator promoted at 300 members scales with the community; a moderation crisis at 3,000 members without one scales too.

The moderation ladder (written down, pinned, boring)

Enforcement that improvises is enforcement that gets called unfair. The standard ladder, from the automation section of the moderation guide: bots catch the mechanical layer — captcha on join (Rose or Shieldy), obvious spam deleted, link floods filtered. Humans handle the human layer with graduated steps: 1) a public one-line nudge; 2) /warn (three warnings auto-mute for 24 hours); 3) a short /mute for heat without malice; 4) /ban for scams, rings and doxxing — always with the reason stated. The multiplier that makes this work is predictability: a pinned ladder turns every moderation decision into "the rule", not "the moderator's mood", and complaints get answered with the pin instead of an argument. Review the ladder quarterly — as the community ages, the violations change shape.

The feedback engine: questions, rituals and the weekly beat

Communities die of silence, not of conflict — most members never post unless something pulls them. The pulls that work: the weekly ritual (the same feature, same day: wins Monday, stupid-questions Friday, the monthly "what should we cover" poll) — rituals give lurkers a known moment to surface; answerable questions — channel posts that end with a choice, not an essay prompt ("A or B?" beats "thoughts?"); the first-reply rule — no question sits unanswered for more than a few hours, because the speed of the first reply predicts whether a second question ever gets asked; and visible impact — when a member's suggestion changes the channel, say so by name. Members who see their fingerprints on the community become its glue. At 1,000+ members, add the structure layer: topics for the big chat, or a small breakout group for the regulars who carry the culture.

Conflict triage: the four fires

Community conflict comes in four shapes, and each has a different tool. The blowup (a heated thread forming): slow mode on, one de-escalating channel post, take it to DMs if two people are locked in — public threads never resolve, they just recruit. The chronic complainer: one direct conversation about what would change their mind; if nothing would, stop engaging — the group watches how you handle this more than anything. The value-drain (someone whose every post makes the room worse without breaking a rule): the quiet tools exist — mute, restricted mode — use them without ceremony. The pile-on (the group against one member): this is the one you act on fast, because it's the culture-defining moment; protect the target publicly, privately tell the pile-on leaders to stand down, and post the boundary afterward as a rule. Communities remember their worst week. Make sure it's handled well.

The founder's trap (and the handoff ladder)

Every healthy community eventually confronts the same bottleneck: everything routes through one person, and that person burns out or vanishes. The systems that prevent it are unglamorous: documented ops — the posting calendar, the moderation ladder and the bot configs written down where a co-admin can find them (a scheduler with stored drafts and queues means the channel publishes correctly even when the founder is offline for a week); a co-admin with real rights by month six — not as a favor but as continuity insurance; the founder's manual — a one-page document: what this community is, who the regulars are, what the rituals are, where the bodies are buried. Communities that survive their founder's vacation, job change or burnout were all built the same way: deliberately redundant from the start.

The metrics of a living community

Channel metrics (views, ERR) barely apply to the group side. The numbers that matter for a community: week-4 activity — of the members who joined this month, what share has said or reacted to anything (5–10% active is normal for a healthy group; below 2% it's a graveyard with notifications); the answer latency — median time before a member question gets any reply (hours, not days); the regulars count — the ~20 people who produce most of the conversation, tracked by name, because losing two of them changes the whole room; and mod actions per week — trending up means a spam problem, spiking after a promo means the promo audience, flat means healthy. Fifteen minutes a week on these four numbers is the difference between managing a community and discovering its autopsy.

faq.q: How many moderators does a Telegram community need?
faq.a: A practical rule: one active moderator per 500–1,000 active members, with a minimum of two humans who can act (never rely on the founder alone — illness and vacations happen). Bots handle the mechanical layer regardless of size: captcha, link filters and obvious spam deletion scale infinitely, which is why the human count stays low while the bot count stays at one or two.

faq.q: Should the discussion group have topics enabled?
faq.a: Not at first — topics add a click of friction, and small communities live on drive-by replies. Switch topics on when the single-thread room becomes genuinely hard to follow, which usually shows up somewhere past a few hundred active members: questions getting buried within minutes, regulars asking for channels by topic. When you do, create few topics (five or so) and pin the mapping — too many topics fragments a community faster than no topics at all.

faq.q: How do I deal with a member who dominates every conversation?
faq.a: First check whether the dominance is actually harmful — a prolific regular who answers questions is a feature, not a bug, even if they are loud. If it is harmful (they crowd out others, make every thread about them), talk to them directly once, specifically, with examples. If nothing changes, use the quiet tools: restricted mode with a timer, or slow mode for the whole group, which spreads the floor without a public confrontation.

faq.q: Can a community survive without the founder being active daily?
faq.a: Yes — if the systems exist: a scheduler running the channel rhythm from a filled queue, co-admins with real rights, a pinned moderation ladder, and rituals that run on a schedule rather than on the founder’s presence. Members stay for the other members, not for the founder, once the culture is set — the founder’s real job is building the machine that makes them unnecessary.

telegram-automation-guide-2026.title: The Complete Telegram Automation Guide for 2026: From First Bot to Self-Updating Channel
telegram-automation-guide-2026.desc: Every automation layer a Telegram channel can have — scheduling, feeds, moderation, cross-posting, analytics — with the architecture that stays reliable, the invariants that prevent disasters, and what never to automate.
telegram-automation-guide-2026.content:
Every channel owner ends up automating something — the question is whether it happens accidentally, one fragile script at a time, or deliberately, as an architecture. This is the deliberate version: every automation layer a Telegram channel can have in 2026, the order to adopt them, the one invariant that keeps the whole system safe, and the failure modes that take down automations that looked solid. The goal is a channel that keeps its voice while the plumbing runs itself.

The layer map: what can be automated, in adoption order

Layer 1 — publishing (adopt first, saves the most stress): every post goes through a scheduler's queue — ManyBot, ControllerBot, Fast Scheduler, whatever fits — so publishing stops depending on someone remembering. The queue view replaces the mental load, and the weekly review becomes possible because next week is already visible. Layer 2 — intake: sources flow into a review chat automatically — RSS bridges for feeds, form-to-chat bridges for submissions, forwarding rules for the channels you monitor. Nothing publishes from intake; it arrives. Layer 3 — moderation: captcha-on-join, link filters and duplicate detection (Rose, Shieldy, Combot) run unsupervised; humans handle the ladder above them. Layer 4 — distribution: cross-posting to sister channels or out to other platforms, through one writer. Layer 5 — measurement: weekly stats collection, ERR tracking, the ritual report — a spreadsheet fed by exports beats a dashboard nobody opens. Five layers, adopted in this order, take a channel from personality-driven to system-driven in about a quarter.

The single-writer rule: the invariant that prevents disasters

Every automation horror story traces to one violation: two systems that both believe they own the publishing tap. The fix is an invariant worth writing on a sticky note: every channel has exactly one writer — a human in the composer or one bot, never both, and nothing else holds admin rights to post. Everything else is upstream of the writer: feeds and forms flow into the review chat, drafts flow into the scheduler, analytics reads what published. Audit it quarterly: list every bot with post rights in every channel and ask, for each, "is this the writer?" — any answer that isn't yes-or-expired-rights is a duplicate-post accident waiting for a quiet week to happen in. Related hygiene: when you retire a tool, revoke its rights the same day (a live token in an abandoned tool is a safety issue, not clutter) — BotFather's /revoke takes ten seconds.

Idempotency: the boring property that saves reputations

Automations fail and get retried — the professional property that makes retries safe is idempotency: the same input applied twice produces one post, not two. The classic failure is the RSS bridge that re-reads a feed after a GUID change and republishes everything as new, overnight, to four thousand people. Defenses, cheapest first: bridges that deduplicate on the feed's item ID (most decent ones do — verify yours by re-adding a feed once and watching); a duplicate check in your review flow (search the channel for the headline before promoting); and the queue as the last gate — a post that already exists in the queue shouldn't be addable again. You can't prevent every double-publish, but you can make them rare enough that the apology post stays hypothetical.

The failure modes that take real channels down

Automations fail silently, which is what makes them dangerous. The gallery: the DST drift — daylight saving moves the "9:00" post to 10:00 for a month before anyone notices (fix: pin the channel's home timezone in the scheduler; check one scheduled post after each clock change). The regenerated token — a token revoken in BotFather turns every dependent tool mute at once (fix: the weekly ping command in your health check). The silent bridge death — a source site changes its feed structure and your intake quietly goes empty (fix: the Friday queue check includes "did intake arrive this week?"). The rate-limit wall — a broadcast bot that ignores retry_after gets throttled for hours mid-announcement (fix: tools that queue and back off properly — roughly one message per second per chat is the ceiling). Each failure is findable in two minutes a week, which is what the health check below actually is.

The weekly health check (five checks, two minutes)

1) The queue — next week's slots exist and nothing is scheduled into dead hours. 2) The published log — last week's posts show no duplicates, no dead-hour sends, no naked-markdown accidents. 3) The ping — send each automation bot one status command; anything that doesn't answer gets fixed before it matters. 4) Intake freshness — the review chat received material this week. 5) The trend — ERR against last week, leaves against the month. Two minutes every Friday; every item on this list has caught a real failure on real channels before the audience saw it. The health check is the price automation charges for its convenience, and it's the cheapest insurance in the whole stack.

What never to automate

The list is short because it's important. The voice: AI-assisted drafts are a tool, but posts that published without a human reading them will eventually embarrass the channel — the approval gate is one tap and it's the whole job. Community replies: automated welcome messages and canned answers read as absence; members can smell the difference, and the first ten seconds of a conversation set its ceiling. Apologies and corrections: when something goes wrong, the response must be human — automating sincerity is sincerity's cancellation. And the decision itself: automation decides when, how and in what order things publish; it should never decide whether — the publish button's human is the channel's editor, and keeping that seat occupied is what keeps a self-updating channel from becoming a self-deleting one.

faq.q: Which automation should a small channel set up first?
faq.a: Scheduling, without question. Moving all posts through a queue is an afternoon of work, costs nothing, and removes the most damaging failure mode small channels have — the forgotten posting day that breaks the habit loop. Intake automation and moderation bots come next, in that order; cross-posting is rarely worth it until there are two worthwhile destinations.

faq.q: How do I stop my RSS bot from double-posting?
faq.a: Use a bridge that deduplicates on the feed item ID, re-add one of your feeds once as a test and watch what happens, and route automated items through a review chat rather than straight to the channel. If a feed keeps regenerating IDs, filter it out — that source is not bridge-safe, and no amount of retry logic will make it one.

faq.q: Is it safe to give one bot all the admin rights?
faq.a: It is safe only if that bot is your writer and the rights match its job: a scheduler needs post and edit rights, nothing more. Distribution of rights should follow the single-writer rule — one bot publishes, moderation bots live only in the discussion group with moderation rights, and analytics bots need to read, not post. Quarterly, revoke anything whose purpose you cannot name.

faq.q: Can AI writing tools run a Telegram channel end to end?
faq.a: They can draft, summarize feeds and fill template slots — and channels that publish AI output unreviewed develop a noticeable voice drift that audiences and advertisers both detect. The working pattern is AI-prepared, human-approved: drafts enter the queue, a person edits and releases. The voice is the product; automation can surround it, but the moment it replaces the reading human, the channel starts dying politely.

telegram-monetization-mistakes.title: The 5 Monetization Mistakes That Kill Telegram Channels
telegram-monetization-mistakes.desc: The money decisions that destroy channels in hindsight — launching too early, pricing from subscriber count, the discount spiral, mixed payment rails — and the sequencing that avoids all five.
telegram-monetization-mistakes.content:
Channel monetization failures are weirdly consistent: the same five mistakes show up in every post-mortem, and all five are visible in advance. None of them are about choosing the wrong model — ads, Stars, subscriptions, affiliate and your own product all work at the right moment. They're about sequencing, pricing psychology and trust accounting. Here they are, with the sequencing that avoids each.

Mistake 1: launching monetization before retention exists

The instinct says strike while the feed is hot; the data says monetization tests your ERR before it tests your audience's wallet. A channel with a 40% ERR can run one promo post in ten and lose nothing measurable; the same promo on a 15% ERR channel visibly accelerates the slide — the audience was already half-gone, and selling to them is what finished the job. The prerequisite, concretely: three months of stable or rising ERR, a weekly open habit you can see in view patterns, and at least one format the audience demonstrably loves (forwards are the receipt). If that list reads like your channel's opposite, monetization isn't the next project — retention is. Money amplifies whatever exists; it does not create an audience that wants to hear from you.

Mistake 2: pricing from the subscriber count

The owner of 10,000 subscribers asks "what do 10k channels charge?" — and anchors to a number that describes the wrong asset. Advertisers buy expected views (ERR × subscribers), audience quality and niche buying power; two 10k channels in the same niche can differ five-fold in real price because one holds a 35% ERR and the other a 7% one that giveaway traffic diluted. The correct pricing sequence: compute expected views, find your niche's per-view band from comparable public channels (TGStat's ERR data makes this a ten-minute exercise), set a floor you won't go under, and put the subscriber count last where it belongs — as a sanity check, not an input. Owners who price from the count systematically underprice strong channels and overprice weak ones; the market quietly fixes both, at your expense.

Mistake 3: the discount spiral

The first sponsor negotiates 30% off, the second hears about it, the third assumes the list price was fiction — six months later the channel runs ads at half its healthy rate and can't climb back, because ad pricing is remembered, not re-derived. The defenses are structural, not heroic: a written rate card (even a two-line one) that exists outside negotiations; value added instead of price cut when pushing back is wrong — a bundle, a second slot, a longer runtime; and the two-strikes rule — discounts happen for strategic reasons (a flagship sponsor, a test slot) at most twice a year, never in consecutive negotiations. The same spiral applies to your own products: the Star-priced guide you sold at 50% off in month one set its real price in every buyer's mind. Channels that hold their pricing signal scarcity and confidence, and both compound.

Mistake 4: mixing the rails (and the money)

Stars for one product, CryptoBot invoices for another, a friend's bank transfer for a third, a subscription bot for a fourth — each works alone, and together they create the three costs owners never budgeted: reconciliation debt (four ledgers, none matching, tax season becomes archaeology), support debt (every rail has its own failure modes and refund flows — you become the payments department for each), and trust erosion (buyers who paid three different ways for three products wonder which one is real). The fix is one primary rail per product type: Stars for low-friction digital goods, one processor for subscriptions, one method for big tickets — and a single ledger sheet from day one (date, product, rail, gross, net). Two rails is a strategy; five is an accident that pays worse than either.

Mistake 5: treating the first sponsor as the ceiling

The channel lands its first paid placement, celebrates, and then... waits for the next inquiry, which comes when it comes. The mistake is structural: sponsorships are a pipeline, not a mailbox. The channels that grow ad income quarter over quarter all do the same boring things: they keep a one-page media kit with public-stat screenshots updated monthly; they proactively pitch adjacent products with a specific slot ("your tool + our Tuesday deep-dive slot in March") instead of advertising availability; they send a delivery report within 24 hours of every placement (views, clicks, the honest sentence on fit) — because renewal is cheaper than acquisition; and they sell the calendar, offering the next open slot by date, which converts scarcity into urgency without a single fake countdown. A sponsorship program is a sales funnel with five stages; channels that run all five double their ad revenue at the same audience size, which is the cheapest growth in the entire monetization catalog.

The order that works

Sequencing solves what willpower can't. The pattern that reliably ends well: months 0–3 — no monetization at all; build the habit, the ERR floor and the formats (the audience remembers what the channel was before it sold anything). Months 3–6 — the soft layer: Stars tips on the best posts, one affiliate mention inside genuinely useful content, nothing that interrupts. Months 6–12 — the structured layer: a rate card, one to two dedicated sponsor slots a month maximum, a delivery report after each. Year two — the owned layer: the paid product or membership built on a year of trust data about what this audience actually pays for. Every layer assumes the previous one's trust was banked and spent slowly — that's the whole secret, and it's why the five mistakes above are all, at root, the same mistake: spending trust faster than the channel earns it.

faq.q: How many subscribers do I need before monetizing a Telegram channel?
faq.a: There is no magic number — the real threshold is engagement, not size: three months of stable or rising ERR, a visible daily-open habit and at least one format that reliably earns forwards. A 2,000-subscriber channel with 45 percent ERR and a loyal niche monetizes better than a 15,000 one at 8 percent. That said, practical ad deals become routine somewhere past a few thousand real, engaged subscribers, because advertisers want meaningful absolute reach too.

faq.q: What is a realistic starting rate card for channel promos?
faq.a: Compute expected views first (ERR times subscribers), then apply your niche’s per-view band — crypto, finance and B2B tools sit at the top, entertainment at the bottom. As a rough anchor, a 5,000-subscriber channel with 30 percent ERR in a mid-value niche starts around $30–120 per dedicated post. Set a floor you will not go under, and raise prices 20–30 percent only when your last three placements have all sold.

faq.q: Should I use Telegram Stars or an external payment provider?
faq.a: Use Stars where friction matters most — small digital goods, tips and paid posts, because the purchase happens inside Telegram in two taps. Use an external rail for subscriptions and bigger tickets where recurring billing, invoices or fiat settlement matter. The mistake is not choosing one over the other — it is running five rails at once, which multiplies reconciliation and support debt for no extra revenue.

faq.q: How do I approach sponsors instead of waiting for inquiries?
faq.a: Pitch specific, not general: name the product, the slot and the date (“your analytics tool in our March 12 teardown slot”), attach a one-page media kit with public-stat screenshots, and lead with one concrete audience-fit sentence. Follow up once after a week, and after every delivered placement send a 24-hour delivery report — sponsors renew on certainty, and the renewal conversation starts the day the first post performs.

fast-scheduler-referral-program-beta.title: Fast Scheduler Referral Program (Beta): Earn Premium Days for Invites
fast-scheduler-referral-program-beta.desc: How the Fast Scheduler referral program works: why unlocking needs a connected channel plus one scheduled message, how both sides earn 3 Premium days, limits, and what beta status means for you.
fast-scheduler-referral-program-beta.content:
Fast Scheduler has a referral program, currently in beta: invite channel owners, and both you and the newcomer earn 3 Premium days for every qualifying referral, up to 15 referees (45 days total). Your personal link lives in the bot under /referral or Premium → Referral Program. This guide explains the two things that confuse people most: why the program stays locked until you verify, and exactly when the days land in your balance.

Why unlocking requires a channel plus one message

Open the referral menu on a fresh account and you will see a lock screen instead of your link: connect your channel and schedule at least one message first. This is deliberate, and it is the same bar for everyone. Premium days cost real money — every gifted day is server time and Telegram Stars fees paid out of our pocket. Without a verification step, anyone could generate dozens of empty accounts in an afternoon and drain the reward pool, which would force us to kill the program for honest users too.

Connecting a channel proves you have somewhere real to post; scheduling a message proves you actually use the bot. Together they take about two minutes: send your channel link in Step 1 of the tutorial, then schedule any post — even a test message counts. We check anonymous counters only (channels connected, messages created). We never read message contents, never ask for documents, and never share anything with third parties. Verification is about activity, not identity.

How crediting works, click to days

1) Click. A newcomer opens your link and starts the bot. The click is recorded instantly, but nothing is granted yet — this pending state is what you see in your referral list before they qualify.

2) Verify. The newcomer connects their channel and schedules their first message, exactly like you did. Until then, the referral stays pending — no matter how long ago they clicked.

3) Credit. The moment they qualify, both sides receive 3 Premium days automatically. Yours land in the referral balance (Available days in /referral). If you already pay for Premium, earned days wait in the balance until the paid period ends.

4) Activate. On the free plan, activate earned days from the referral menu and a Premium period starts immediately. Used days move to the Used counter, so earned, used and available totals are always visible.

Rules that protect the program

The referred user must be genuinely new and must arrive via your link as their first interaction. One referral per user — the same newcomer can never credit you twice. Fake accounts created to farm days do not qualify, and farmed balances can be removed. These rules are enforced automatically; disputes go to @MaximalXP.

What beta means for you

Beta status affects polish, never balances. Links, tracking, crediting and activation are all live, but you may meet rough edges: a counter that updates with a delay, a list that needs a reopen to refresh. Earned days are recorded the moment they qualify and are never lost to a display glitch — reopen /referral first if a number looks stale. Reward sizes and limits can still be tuned during beta; anything you already earned is honored under the rules that were live when you earned it. Spotted something odd? Send it via /feedback with step-by-step text and a screenshot — beta reports shape the final version.

faq.q: Why is my referral menu locked?
faq.a: The program unlocks after you connect a channel and schedule at least one message. This verifies your account is genuine before you can earn rewards. Both steps take about two minutes inside the bot tutorial.

faq.q: When do I get my Premium days for a referral?
faq.a: When your referee connects their channel and schedules their first message. At that moment both of you receive 3 Premium days automatically — yours appear under Available days in /referral.

faq.q: Is there a limit to referral earnings?
faq.a: Yes: up to 15 referees, i.e. 45 Premium days total, and one credit per newcomer. Paid Premium subscribers bank earned days in their balance until the paid period ends.

faq.q: Are my earned days safe while the program is in beta?
faq.a: Yes. Beta affects polish, not balances: every qualifying referral is recorded immediately, and earned days are honored even if reward rules are tuned later. Report glitches via /feedback.

media-storage-premium-toolkit.title: Media Storage Goes Pro: Move, Copy and Download Whole Boxes
media-storage-premium-toolkit.desc: Fast Scheduler Media Storage learned bulk moves: Move All and Copy All with type filters plus whole-box download as one archive. What each tool does, when to use it, and what stays free.
media-storage-premium-toolkit.content:
Media Storage started as a simple shelf: save a photo once, reuse it in any post. It worked — until libraries grew into hundreds of files across a dozen boxes and reorganizing meant tapping through every item one by one. The Premium toolkit fixes exactly that with three bulk tools: Move All, Copy All, and Download Box.

Move All: reorganize a box in one tap

Open any box and tap Move All. Every item goes to the box you pick — or only one type, with the optional filter for images, videos, or files. The classic use: a mixed “everything” box that grew for months gets split by type in three taps. Another: retiring a finished campaign — move the whole box into an archive box and the working set is clean again. ControllerBot and ManyBot make you do this file by file; here it is one action.

Copy All: seed without touching the original

Copy All follows the same flow, but the source box keeps its items. That is the right tool when a new campaign needs the same starter set — brand banner, price card, disclaimer image — without disturbing the archive they live in. Filter by type the same way: copy only the videos into a video-only box, for example.

Download Box: the whole box as one archive

Download Box packs the entire box into a single archive. Keep an offline copy before a big restructuring, hand a full asset set to a teammate or designer, or pull everything down before travel. One archive beats twenty forwarded files — names, quality, and order survive the trip.

What stays free

Everything, one file at a time: open any item and Move, Copy, or Download works on the Free plan with no limits on how often. Premium only removes the repetition — the same results, minus the tapping. If your library fits in one box of 100 items and you rarely reorganize, Free remains the right plan.

A cleanup routine that actually sticks

Once a quarter: open each box, Move All by type into sorted boxes, Download Box for the ones you are retiring, delete what is left. Ten minutes, four times a year, and the picker stays a joy instead of an archaeology dig.

faq.q: Are Move All, Copy All and Download Box Premium-only?
faq.a: Yes. On Free you can move, copy, and download items one at a time with no usage limits — Premium only adds the bulk versions.

faq.q: Can I move only videos or only photos between boxes?
faq.a: Yes. Move All and Copy All offer an optional type filter (images, videos, files), so a single tap can split a mixed box by type.

faq.q: What exactly do I get when I download a box?
faq.a: One archive containing the box files — for offline backup, restructuring safety, or handing assets to a teammate.

faq.q: How many boxes and items does Premium allow?
faq.a: Up to 20 boxes with 500 items each, videos included (up to 50MB), and uploads to 100 MB. Free keeps 1 box with 100 items, no video in storage.

october-2026-legal-refresh.title: Our October 2026 Legal Refresh: What Changed and Where to Find It
october-2026-legal-refresh.desc: Privacy Policy, Terms and Refund Policy rewritten for clarity in October 2026: what changed, what stayed the same, and where every past version lives.
october-2026-legal-refresh.content:
In October 2026 we rewrote all three legal documents — Privacy Policy, Terms of Service, and Refund Policy. Nothing about the product changed: no new data collection, no new fees, no change to what the bot does. The goal was clarity: shorter sentences, explicit service names, and every past version kept public so changes are auditable.

Privacy Policy: explicit services, same rights

The policy now names each service it covers — Fast Scheduler, the SetDate companion bot, the Support bot, and this website — and lists exactly what is stored and why: your Telegram user ID, connected channel IDs, scheduled messages, settings, and bot tokens. Media stays as Telegram file references, never re-uploaded copies. Your rights are unchanged: export a copy anytime, and delete everything on request. Nothing is sold, and nothing leaves the pipeline except payment processing via Telegram.

Terms: clearer rules, announced changes

Plan limits, fair-use rules, and account safety are now stated plainly, including how future changes work: material changes (pricing, data processing, user rights) are announced in-app, and continued use after the effective date means acceptance. Non-material fixes just update the revision date. If you ever disagree with an update, export or delete your data first — both are one request away.

Refund Policy: Stars rules, stated plainly

Premium is paid in Telegram Stars, and Stars purchases are final under Telegram's own policies — the new text says so outright instead of implying it. Outside mandatory consumer rights, refunds are discretionary and case by case: double charges and genuine technical faults are the classic approved cases. Requests go to fastschedulebot@gmail.com with the transaction ID, username, and reason, and we acknowledge within 7 business days. Monthly plans still cancel via /premium with the paid period running to its end date.

Where past versions live

Every document shows its effective date, and previous versions stay published in the version history on the website, reachable from the legal pages. When the next refresh comes, you will be able to diff it yourself instead of taking our word for it.

faq.q: Do I need to accept the updated policies?
faq.a: No extra tap is needed. Material changes are announced in-app, and continued use after the effective date means acceptance. If you disagree, stop using the service after exporting or deleting your data.

faq.q: Where can I read the previous versions?
faq.a: On the website under the legal pages’ version history. Every past version stays published with its effective date.

faq.q: Did the refund rules change in October 2026?
faq.a: The new text states the standing practice plainly: Telegram Stars purchases are final, with discretionary case-by-case refunds for genuine failures. Requests go to fastschedulebot@gmail.com.

qa_fsback_vs_fspback.title: What Is the Difference Between .fsback and .fspback?
qa_fsback_vs_fspback.desc: Fast Scheduler saves backups as .fsback or .fspback files. Here is exactly what each format contains, when to pick which, and how to restore them.
qa_fsback_vs_fspback.content:
Short answer: both are the same complete backup — the only difference is the password. A .fspback file is a password-protected .fsback file. The extra “p” stands for protected.

What each format is

  • .fsback — a full backup of your Fast Scheduler data with no password. Anyone who gets the file can restore it, so treat it like a plain-text secret.
  • .fspback — the same backup, encrypted. Restoring asks for the password you set when creating it. Without the password the data inside cannot be read.

When you tap Create Backup (or send /backup), the bot asks whether you want password protection. Choosing no password produces .fsback; setting a password (and an optional hint) produces .fspback. A Premium feature — backups are part of the Export & Backup toolkit that unlocks with Premium.

What is inside either file

Both formats package your selected data — scheduled messages, recurring messages, settings, and more — into one archive you can download, store in the cloud, or move to another account. Media you saved in Media Storage is referenced, not re-uploaded, so files stay small.

Which one should you pick?

  • Restoring to your own account right now? .fsback is fine and faster to use.
  • Keeping the file long-term, sending it to a teammate, or migrating to a new phone? .fspback — the password protects your scheduled content from strangers.

Restoring a file

Send /import to the bot, attach the .fsback or .fspback file, enter the password if asked, then choose Overwrite (replace current data) or Add (merge with current data). Export a fresh backup before you overwrite anything.

faq.q: Is .fspback more secure than .fsback?
faq.a: Yes. A .fspback file is encrypted with the password you set; a .fsback file is not protected at all. If the backup contains bot tokens or private content, prefer .fspback.

faq.q: I lost the password to my .fspback file. Can it be recovered?
faq.a: No. The password cannot be reset or bypassed — not even by support. Keep the password (and the hint you optionally set) together with the file. Without it the backup is unreadable.

faq.q: Can I convert .fsback to .fspback (or back)?
faq.a: Indirectly: restore the .fsback file into your account, then create a new backup and choose password protection to get a .fspback file. There is no direct file-conversion command.

faq.q: Which formats can I import besides these?
faq.a: Imports also accept .json, .csv, .txt, .rtf and .odt files (and SetDate bundles). Those carry messages only, while .fsback/.fspback carry your full configuration.

qa_backup_full_guide.title: How to Back Up All Scheduled Posts in Telegram (and Restore Them Anywhere)
qa_backup_full_guide.desc: A complete, human-friendly guide to backing up scheduled Telegram posts with Fast Scheduler: what gets saved, password protection, cloud storage of files, and clean restore.
qa_backup_full_guide.content:
Rebuilding a month of scheduled posts by hand is nobody's idea of fun. Fast Scheduler's backup system exists so you never have to: one file captures everything, and restoring it on any account takes about a minute.

What a backup contains

A .fsback / .fspback file packages the parts of your account you select — typically:

  • Scheduled messages — every queued post with its exact send time.
  • Recurring messages — repeat rules (daily, weekly, custom intervals) and their expiry settings.
  • Settings — language, time zone, signatures, channel preferences.
  • Media Storage references — saved photos, videos and documents with their boxes.

What is not included: user backups exclude sender-bot tokens, and payment history never leaves Telegram's systems. The export screen lets you review what goes into the file before you confirm.

Creating a backup — step by step

Backups are a Premium feature. With Premium active:

  • 1. Open the menu → Data → Export (or send /backup).
  • 2. Pick what to include (scheduled, recurring, all).
  • 3. Choose password protection: none for .fsback, or set a password + hint for .fspback.
  • 4. The bot packs the archive and sends the file. Save it somewhere real — cloud drive, local disk, anywhere that survives losing your phone.

Restoring — the safe way

Send /import, attach the file, enter the password if prompted. The bot then asks how to apply it:

  • Overwrite — replaces your current data with the backup's content. Anything not in the backup disappears.
  • Add — merges the backup into your current data, keeping what you already have.

Golden rule: export a fresh backup before restoring an older one. It is your undo button if the result surprises you.

Good backup habits

  • Take a fresh backup before deleting a channel, rotating a bot, or bulk-editing posts.
  • Keep at least one .fspback with a strong password — shared drives get opened by more people than you think.
  • After switching phones or accounts, restore + verify the Message List before the real posting week starts.

faq.q: Is backup free or Premium?
faq.a: Creating .fsback/.fspback backups is part of the Export & Backup toolkit, which requires Premium. Importing files (/import) works on Free, so anyone can restore a backup received from someone else.

faq.q: Where should I store the backup file?
faq.a: Anywhere outside Telegram: a cloud drive, your computer, or an encrypted notes app. Telegram keeps the file in your chat too, but Saved Messages is not a backup strategy.

faq.q: How big is a backup file?
faq.a: Small — usually kilobytes to a few megabytes, because media is referenced rather than embedded. Text and schedules compress extremely well.

faq.q: Can I move my schedules to another Telegram account?
faq.a: Yes. Create a backup on the old account, log into the new one, connect the channel and a sender bot, then restore the backup with Add mode. This is the standard migration path.

qa_move_channel_account.title: How to Move Fast Scheduler to a New Phone or Another Telegram Account
qa_move_channel_account.desc: Step-by-step migration guide: back up, reconnect the channel and sender bot, restore schedules on a new device or account — without losing posting times.
qa_move_channel_account.content:
Fast Scheduler stores your schedules in the cloud (on the bot's server), not on your phone. That makes moving house surprisingly painless — the only thing that really matters is which Telegram account owns the schedules.

Same account, new phone

Do nothing. Open Telegram on the new phone, log in, and chat with @FastSchedulerBot — your channels, bots, schedules and settings are exactly where you left them. There is no local app and nothing to sync.

Different account (new number, team handover, second project)

Schedules belong to the Telegram account that created them, so a new account starts empty. The clean path:

  • 1. On the old account: /backup → include everything → save the .fsback/.fspback file.
  • 2. On the new account: /start the bot, connect the channel, then pair its sender bot (this is mandatory — the sender bot is what actually posts).
  • 3. Send /import with the backup file, choose Add or Overwrite.
  • 4. Check the Message List and Calendar; confirm the time zone matches, then skim the first few upcoming posts.

If you are on Free and your setup has more than one channel, temporarily move the extra channels out or upgrade — the restore brings everything over, but Free limits apply on the new account.

Handing a channel to someone else permanently

The same flow works for handovers: the new owner connects their own account to the same channel (they need admin rights in it), pairs a sender bot, and imports the backup you send them. After they confirm the Message List looks right, you can delete your own schedules to avoid double-posting — two accounts scheduling the same channel will post twice.

faq.q: Will my schedules keep firing while I migrate?
faq.a: Yes — the old account keeps posting until you delete its schedules or the channel/bot setup changes. Pause or delete there before going live on the new account to avoid duplicates.

faq.q: Do I need Premium on the new account to restore?
faq.a: No. Importing a backup is free. Premium is only needed for creating backups and for the extra channels/bots the backup may contain.

qa_duplicate_posts.title: Why Is My Telegram Channel Posting Twice? (Duplicate Posts, Explained)
qa_duplicate_posts.desc: Duplicated scheduled posts almost always mean two schedulers own the channel, or a sender bot got re-added. Here is how to find the cause and stop double-posting.
qa_duplicate_posts.content:
Double posts are annoying for subscribers and make a channel look automated in the worst way. The good news: the cause is nearly always one of four things.

1. Another account still schedules the channel

The most common cause after a migration or team handover: the old account's schedules were never removed. Both accounts happily queue posts for the same time. Fix: in the other account, open Message List and delete its schedules (or disconnect the channel). If you cannot access the old account, remove the bot from the channel's admin list — that stops the posting immediately.

2. Two sender bots are admin in the channel

Every channel must pair with exactly one sender bot, and that bot should be the only bot with posting rights. If you created a second bot and added it as admin, posts may arrive from both. Keep one sender bot per channel as admin; remove extra bots from the channel.

3. The message got scheduled twice

Easy to do when re-sending the same text after an edit, or when importing while old schedules exist. Open the Message List for the day and scan for same-time twins before the posting window. The Calendar view makes clusters obvious.

4. The recurrence rule was duplicated, not edited

Creating a new daily rule instead of editing the existing one produces two identical posts every day. Check the recurring list — if two rules share the same text and time, delete one.

Still posting twice?

Send /stats to see what is queued, then use /feedback with the channel name and two timestamps of a duplicate pair. Support can trace which connection produced each post.

faq.q: Does Fast Scheduler retry a post that failed, causing doubles?
faq.a: A retry only happens when the send did not confirm. If Telegram accepted the post but the confirmation was lost (rare network hiccup), you can get one duplicate. It does not re-send confirmed posts.

faq.q: Can I merge two accounts scheduling the same channel?
faq.a: Yes — export from the old account, import with Add on the new one, then clear the old account. Never leave both active.

qa_timezones.title: Why Did My Post Go Out at the Wrong Time? Time Zones, Explained Simply
qa_timezones.desc: Scheduled posts firing an hour early or late? The channel time zone, daylight-saving shifts, and per-channel settings explain 99% of these surprises.
qa_timezones.content:
“I scheduled 9:00 and it posted at 12:00” — before anything else, check which clock the number 9:00 belongs to. Fast Scheduler schedules posts in a time zone, and the zone that matters is the one set for the channel, not the one on your watch.

How the bot decides “when 9:00 is”

  • Every channel has a time zone setting. When you schedule 9:00, the bot stores 9:00 in the channel's zone and converts it to UTC behind the scenes.
  • If the zone is UTC (the default) and you are in, say, New York, your 9:00 local is 13:00 or 14:00 UTC — the post will “move” by 4–5 hours from your point of view.
  • Set the channel's zone to your own city once, and from then on 9:00 means your 9:00, every time.

The daylight-saving trap

Zones that observe DST shift twice a year. A post scheduled for 9:00 in March may land at 8:00 or 10:00 relative to the wall clock in November, depending on how the zone handles the shift. If your audience notices a one-hour drift in spring or autumn, that is why. The schedule did not break — the zone's definition of 9:00 changed. Reschedule around the shift week if you post at a strict local hour.

Checking and fixing the zone

Open Time Zone in the bot (or /timezone), pick the channel, and choose the city/zone that matches your audience — the list uses proper zone names like Europe/Berlin, so DST is handled by the same rules your phone uses. Upcoming posts keep their stored times; only new schedules use the new zone, so double-check anything queued for the same day you change it.

Quick diagnosis table

  • Off by a whole number of hours, constant — wrong zone set for the channel.
  • Off by one hour, only in spring/autumn — DST shift; the zone is working correctly.
  • Off by a few minutes, growing over weeks — rare; send /feedback with two examples.

faq.q: Does changing the time zone move my scheduled posts?
faq.a: No. Existing posts keep their stored times; the new zone applies to schedules you create afterwards. Verify the next few posts after changing the zone.

faq.q: What time zone should I pick for an international audience?
faq.a: Pick the zone of your largest audience segment, or UTC if you think in UTC. Consistency matters more than the specific zone.

qa_edit_scheduled_post.title: Can I Edit a Scheduled Post After Scheduling It?
qa_edit_scheduled_post.desc: Yes — text, media, and send time all stay editable until the moment the post goes out. Here is what can be changed, what cannot, and how retries work.
qa_edit_scheduled_post.content:
Nothing about a scheduled post is carved in stone. Until the moment Telegram accepts the send, every part of it can change — that is the whole point of keeping a queue instead of posting immediately.

What you can change

  • Text and formatting — fix a typo, rewrite the hook, add links. Bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, spoilers and code all survive edits.
  • Media — swap the image, replace the video, add or remove an album item.
  • Send time — move the post earlier or later, or to another day entirely.
  • Target channel — re-point a post to a different connected channel.

Open the Message List (or /list), tap the post, choose 🔄 Replace. The familiar schedule flow reopens with the post's current content pre-filled — change what you need and confirm.

What editing cannot do

  • Change a post that already published. Once the sender bot delivers the message to Telegram, it is a normal Telegram message — edit it with Telegram's own tools, not here.
  • Edit recurring posts “in place”. A recurring rule is a single template that fires on its pattern — there are no separate per-day copies. Edit the rule so all future sends change.

A workflow that actually works

Channel operators who stay sane usually: schedule the week on Sunday, review the Calendar Monday, and treat edit as the normal verb — improving copy as the news moves. Edits are free, instant, and never notify subscribers. The only deadline is the send time itself.

faq.q: How late can I edit a post?
faq.a: Any time before the send moment. If the bot is mid-delivery, the edit may not apply — that is the only race. For a post due within seconds, delete and reschedule instead.

faq.q: Can I edit a post that already went out?
faq.a: Not from the bot — it is a regular Telegram message now. Telegram itself lets admins edit posted messages in channels; use Telegram for that.

faq.q: Does editing reset the monthly send counter?
faq.a: No. The counter counts actual sends, not edits. Editing costs nothing.

qa_free_limits.title: What Do I Get With Fast Scheduler for Free? (Exact Limits)
qa_free_limits.desc: The complete Free plan breakdown: 1 channel, 1 sender bot, 100 pending scheduled messages, 100 sends per channel monthly, 1 recurring rule, storage and media caps.
qa_free_limits.content:
Free is a real plan, not a trial — it never expires and has no daily caps. Here is exactly what you get, with numbers you can plan around.

The numbers

  • {channels_free} channel with {bots_free} sender bot.
  • Up to {scheduled_free} scheduled messages pending at once — your working queue. As posts go out, space frees up; this is not a monthly allowance.
  • {monthly_sent_free} sent messages per channel per calendar month — the actual sending quota. Resets on the 1st.
  • {recurring_free} recurring message — one repeating rule (daily, weekly, every N hours…). Recurring rules on Free expire after {recurring_expiry_days} days and need re-confirming.
  • Media Storage: {storage_count_free} box with {storage_items_free} items, no video in storage.
  • Uploads up to {max_media_free}, videos {videos_msg_free}.

What “100/month per channel” means in practice

If you post 3 times a day, that is ~90 posts a month — Free covers a light daily cadence on one channel. Posting 5+ times a day, or running several channels, is where Premium starts to make sense. The counter counts sends by the sender bot; edits, previews and deleted schedules are free.

There is no daily cap

Older versions of the bot had daily limits; they are gone. On Free you can schedule and send every single day — the only quotas are the pending-queue size and the monthly send count. Check both any time with /stats.

Hitting a limit gracefully

The queue limit blocks new schedules, never deletes old ones; the monthly cap pauses sends until the 1st (the bot tells you). Both warn you in advance with clear messages and a one-tap upgrade path. Nothing is silently dropped.

faq.q: Do unused sends carry over to next month?
faq.a: No. The monthly counter resets to zero on the 1st; unused sends do not roll over. The pending-queue space is also not a quota to “use up” — it just caps how far ahead you can stockpile.

faq.q: Is the free plan time-limited or feature-crippled?
faq.a: It never expires. Scheduling, recurring, statistics, search and the calendar all work on Free. Premium removes quantity limits and adds the Export/Backup toolkit, signatures and bigger media.

faq.q: How do I check my current usage?
faq.a: Send /stats. It shows your queue size, monthly sends, recurring rules and storage at a glance.

qa_premium_worth.title: Is Fast Scheduler Premium Worth It? An Honest Breakdown
qa_premium_worth.desc: What Premium actually unlocks — 3 channels, unlimited queue and sends, unlimited recurring, 50MB video, signatures, export/backup — and who genuinely needs it.
qa_premium_worth.content:
Premium costs {premium_monthly} a month (or {premium_yearly} a year) and removes the ceiling on almost everything Free limits. Here is an honest map of who needs which part.

What Premium changes, concretely

  • {channels_prem} channels, {bots_prem} sender bots — run a network (main channel, announcements, chat-announcements mirror) from one account.
  • Unlimited scheduled queue and unlimited sends — no {scheduled_free}-post queue, no monthly cap on any channel.
  • Unlimited recurring rules — and they never expire; Free's single rule stops after {recurring_expiry_days} days.
  • Bigger media: uploads to {max_media_prem}, video to {videos_msg_prem}, {storage_count_prem} storage boxes × {storage_items_prem} items with video allowed, plus 4K-photo handling and higher bitrate media that Free compresses harder.
  • Signatures — a footer (credit, promo, hashtags) auto-appended to every post of a channel.
  • Export & Backup toolkit — .fsback/.fspback backups, JSON/CSV/TXT/RTF/ODT exports: own your content.

Who does not need it

One channel, a couple of posts a day, no video-heavy content — Free covers that indefinitely. Premium's first meaningful gate for such a setup would be the monthly send cap, and even that takes ~4 posts/day to hit.

Who feels the difference on day one

  • Multi-channel admins — the 3×3 pairing is the headline feature.
  • Video channels — 25MB → 50MB video and video-in-storage change the workflow.
  • Anyone whose content is their business — backups and full exports are the difference between “my queue” and “my archive”.
  • Automation lovers — unlimited recurring rules turn the bot into a true publishing engine.

Terms worth knowing

Premium attaches to your Telegram account, covers all your channels at once, and can be paid with Telegram Stars. Multi-month terms cost less per month (3/6-month discounts), and if something goes wrong the refund policy is linked in the footer — premium status is visible any time with /premium.

faq.q: Does Premium apply to all my channels or per channel?
faq.a: Per account. One subscription unlocks the higher limits for every channel you connect while it is active.

faq.q: What happens to my schedules when Premium expires?
faq.a: Nothing is deleted. Limits revert to Free: extra channels/bots beyond 1×1 stop scheduling until you disconnect them or renew, the queue cap applies again, and recurring rules beyond the first pause.

faq.q: Can I pay with Telegram Stars?
faq.a: Yes — Stars are billed at the official rate and are currently the only payment method. The Premium menu always shows current prices.

qa_add_channel_guide.title: How to Connect a Telegram Channel to Fast Scheduler (Full Walkthrough)
qa_add_channel_guide.desc: Every step to connect a channel: admin rights the bot needs, public vs private channels, invite links, sender bot pairing, and fixing the classic errors.
qa_add_channel_guide.content:
Connecting a channel is a two-part handshake: the bot needs admin rights in the channel, and the channel needs to be registered in the bot. Here is the whole dance, including the steps people miss.

Part 1 — make the bot an admin of your channel

  • 1. Open your channel in Telegram → Manage Channel → Administrators → Add Admin.
  • 2. Search for @FastSchedulerBot and add it.
  • 3. Give it at least Post Messages. If you plan to schedule on behalf of other admins or use anonymous admin, keep the defaults sane.

Part 2 — register the channel in the bot

  • 1. In the bot, tap Connect Channel.
  • 2. Give the bot what it asks for — any of these works:
    • the channel's @username for public channels,
    • a forwarded message from the channel,
    • an invite link (t.me/+… or t.me/joinchat/…) for private channels.
  • 3. Confirm. The bot verifies that it really is an admin there.

Part 3 — pair the sender bot (mandatory)

Every channel needs a sender bot — your own bot created via @BotFather — before anything can be scheduled. This is not optional: the sender bot is the account that actually publishes your posts, under its name. Fast Scheduler's main bot coordinates the schedule; the sender bot delivers. The in-bot wizard creates and pairs one in a minute; see the sender-bots guide for the detailed flow.

The classic errors, decoded

  • “Channel not found” — typo in the username, or the bot was not added as admin before you tried to connect. Add first, then connect.
  • “Not an admin” — the admin rights were granted to a different bot than the one you connected.
  • “Invalid token” — the sender-bot token got truncated on copy. Copy the whole thing: digits, colon, the rest.

faq.q: Can I connect a private channel?
faq.a: Yes — via invite link or by forwarding any message from the channel during connection. Public username is not required.

faq.q: Why do I need my own bot just to post?
faq.a: Telegram architecture: messages in a channel are sent by a bot account, not by your user account. Pairing your own sender bot also means posts appear under your brand, not a generic one.

faq.q: The channel connects but posts fail. First checks?
faq.a: Sender bot still admin? Post Messages permission on? Bot not revoked in @BotFather? Those three cover nearly all post failures.

qa_sender_bot_required.title: Do You Need a Sender Bot to Schedule Posts? (Yes — Here Is Why)
qa_sender_bot_required.desc: Fast Scheduler requires a sender bot for every channel: what it does, why the main bot cannot post alone, how to create one in 60 seconds, and security notes.
qa_sender_bot_required.content:
Short answer: yes — a sender bot is required for scheduling and sending. The scheduling menu stays locked until every connected channel has one paired. Here is the why and the 60-second setup.

Why the main bot cannot just post itself

Two reasons, one technical and one yours:

  • Architecture: channel posts are delivered by a bot account with admin rights. If @FastSchedulerBot delivered them, every message on every customer channel would carry the same name — and one bot hitting rate limits would slow thousands of channels.
  • Your brand: with your own sender bot, posts appear from your bot's name and avatar. Subscribers see your brand, and your bot's admin rights are yours to revoke.

Creating one in 60 seconds

  • 1. Open @BotFather → /newbot → pick a name and username.
  • 2. Copy the token (digits, colon, letters — the whole string).
  • 3. In Fast Scheduler: Bots → ➕ Add Another Bot, pick the channel when asked, paste the token. Pairing is automatic.
  • 4. Make the new bot an admin of the channel with Post Messages permission — or let Fast Scheduler promote it automatically when it can. Scheduling unlocks instantly.

The in-bot wizard walks these exact steps and checks each one, so you cannot get the order wrong.

Security, briefly

Your token is stored encrypted and used only to deliver your posts. You can rotate it any time via @BotFather (/revoke) and update it in the bot — or remove the bot entirely, which deletes the token from Fast Scheduler's storage. If a token leaks, revoke it in BotFather first; a revoked token is dead everywhere.

One bot per channel (Premium: 3×3)

Free pairs {bots_free} sender bot with {channels_free} channel; Premium allows {bots_prem} bots across {channels_prem} channels. Multiple channels can share one sender bot, but the clean setup — one bot per channel — keeps branding separate and failures isolated.

faq.q: Can one sender bot serve two channels?
faq.a: Yes, a sender bot can be paired with multiple channels you own. One bot per channel is still recommended for cleaner branding and simpler troubleshooting.

faq.q: What happens if I remove the sender bot from the channel?
faq.a: Scheduling locks (no sender paired for that channel) and queued sends fail until you re-add the bot as admin. The schedules themselves stay saved.

faq.q: Is my bot token safe with Fast Scheduler?
faq.a: Tokens are stored encrypted and never displayed in full after saving. Rotating the token in @BotFather instantly invalidates the old one everywhere.

qa_schedule_many_at_once.title: How to Schedule Many Telegram Posts at Once (Bulk Workflow)
qa_schedule_many_at_once.desc: Three proven ways to schedule in bulk: SetDate import for prepared batches, recurring rules for repeatable slots, and the queue workflow for content weeks.
qa_schedule_many_at_once.content:
Scheduling one post at a time is fine for a meme; for a content calendar you want batch workflows. Fast Scheduler gives you three, and a full week can be set up in minutes.

Way 1 — import a batch with SetDate

The SetDate bot is the bulk tool: prepare messages as a set (text, times), then import them into Fast Scheduler in one click. It shines when you write copy in advance or migrate from another scheduler. Prepare → import → review in the Message List → done.

Way 2 — let recurring rules do the repeating

Anything that repeats should be a rule, not N one-off posts: “every day at 9:00”, “Mondays 18:30”, “every 6 hours”. Premium users get unlimited rules and no expiry; Free has one rule. Combined with a signature, a daily digest literally runs itself.

Way 3 — stock the queue ahead

The queue lets you stack up to {scheduled_free} pending posts on Free (unlimited on Premium). The classic pattern: one writing session → schedule the whole week → check the Calendar view for holes and collisions → go live your life. Edits are free and instant, so the queue is your draft folder as much as your pipeline.

Checking your work

Three tools keep bulk work honest:

  • Calendar — month at a glance; tap a day to see that day's posts.
  • Message List — per-channel queue with previews; catch same-time twins here.
  • Search — keyword search across everything scheduled, with per-result preview and edit for cleanup.

faq.q: Is there a true “upload a CSV of posts” feature?
faq.a: Close: SetDate handles prepared batches, and /import accepts .json/.csv/.txt/.rtf/.odt files of messages. For calendar-scale bulk entry, SetDate is the intended tool.

faq.q: How far ahead can I schedule?
faq.a: As far as your queue limit allows — up to 100 pending posts on Free, unlimited on Premium. Times years out are fine.

tg_channels_explained.title: Telegram Channels vs Groups vs Bots: The Difference That Actually Matters
tg_channels_explained.desc: A plain-English explainer of Telegram channel, group and bot roles — written for people who schedule content, with practical notes on admin rights and posting.
tg_channels_explained.content:
Telegram has three kinds of “places”, and content creators mix them up constantly. Here is the mental model that sticks.

A channel is a megaphone

One-way broadcasting: admins post, subscribers read. No reply threads by default (though a discussion group can be attached), unlimited subscribers, and posts carry the channel's name — or the name of the posting bot if “Sign messages with a bot” is on. Channels are where scheduled content lives.

A group is a campfire

Everyone talks. Groups are for community; up to 200k members in supergroups, full message history, topics if enabled. You do not “schedule to a group” the way you do to a channel — that is what channels are for.

A bot is a worker

Bots are accounts run by software. In your channel's context, a bot is the hands that type the message: a bot must be an admin with Post Messages for anything to be published. That is exactly why Fast Scheduler pairs a sender bot with your channel — your bot posts, under your brand.

Why this matters for scheduling

  • Want posts to appear at fixed times? Channel + scheduler + sender bot.
  • Want subscribers to discuss the posts? Attach a linked discussion group to the channel — comments live there automatically.
  • Want automation, menus, and commands? That is the bot layer — the part Fast Scheduler turns into a full publishing workflow.

One nuance worth knowing: Telegram shows signed posts as “via bot” only when the admin chooses to sign with the bot; otherwise the post simply appears under the channel name. Either way, the sender bot did the typing.

faq.q: Can a scheduled post go to a group?
faq.a: Fast Scheduler targets channels (including chat-announcement channels). Groups are conversational — schedule announcements to a channel instead.

faq.q: Do subscribers see which bot posted?
faq.a: By default a channel post shows just the channel name. If the channel enables signing posts with the admin bot, the sender bot is credited.

tg_best_posting_times.title: The Best Times to Post in Telegram (and How to Test Them Properly)
tg_best_posting_times.desc: Evidence-based posting windows for Telegram channels by audience type, why consistency beats perfect timing, and how to A/B test slots with scheduled posts.
tg_best_posting_times.content:
“Post at 9:00” advice is usually recycled guesswork. Here is what actually moves the needle on Telegram, plus a testing method you can run with a scheduler in one week.

Windows that generally work

  • Morning commute — 8:00–10:00 local time. News, digests, “start of day” content.
  • Lunch dip — 12:30–14:00. Light, skimmable posts do well.
  • Evening prime time — 19:00–22:00. The strongest window for most channels; long-form and media belong here.

The key word is local. If your audience spans zones, anchor to your largest cluster's evening, and let the channel's time zone setting do the conversion for you.

Consistency beats cleverness

Subscribers learn your rhythm. A channel that posts daily at 9:00 trains its audience to show up at 9:00 — measurable in view-rate stability. This is the strongest argument for scheduling (and recurring rules) over manual posting: the schedule becomes a product feature.

How to test slots properly

  • 1. Pick two candidate slots (e.g. 9:00 vs 20:00) and alternate similar content between them for 7–10 days.
  • 2. Compare views in the first hour, not totals — that is when your regulars arrive. Fast Scheduler's statistics screen shows view dynamics per post.
  • 3. Keep the winner as a recurring rule, and re-test quarterly. Audiences drift with seasons and habits.

Small things that quietly help

  • Don't stack posts 5 minutes apart — spacing beats bursts for notification fatigue.
  • Media posts slightly outperform text-only at equal times in most niches.
  • Skip the “dump 6 posts at midnight” pattern; Telegram's own limits and your subscribers' patience both prefer a steady drip.

faq.q: Does Telegram show “time of post” that I can use for testing?
faq.a: Views are timestamped; compare first-hour views across slots. The statistics screen gives you per-post numbers without extra tools.

faq.q: How many posts per day is healthy?
faq.a: 2–4 for most content channels. Beyond that, watch unsubscribes — the metric that punishes oversharing fastest.

qa_pay_stars_crypto.title: How to Pay for Fast Scheduler Premium (Stars and What Happens After)
qa_pay_stars_crypto.desc: Paying for Premium step by step: Telegram Stars at the official rate, plan terms, activation timing, and what to do if payment succeeded but nothing changed.
qa_pay_stars_crypto.content:
Premium attaches to your Telegram account and covers every channel you connect while it is active. Payment lives in the bot's Premium menu and uses Telegram Stars only.

Telegram Stars

Stars are Telegram's in-app currency. The bot converts the USD price at the official rate and shows the exact Star amount before you confirm — buy Stars in Telegram if your balance is short, approve, and Premium activates the moment the invoice clears. Refunds of Stars purchases follow Telegram's own flow, which is also why the bot asks you to double-check the term before paying.

Plan terms

The monthly Stars plan renews automatically until cancelled. Prepaid 3-month, 6-month, and yearly plans are one-time purchases (with up-front 3/6-month discounts) and never auto-renew.

Right after payment

  • Premium flags appear instantly in the menus; /premium shows status and expiry date.
  • If you paid but see no change: restart the bot with /start — status is refreshed on launch. Still stuck? /feedback with the payment date and method gets a human on it the same day.

Terms, renewals, refunds

Multi-month terms cost proportionally less (built-in 3/6-month discounts), and expiry is shown everywhere Premium matters. When a prepaid term ends, limits quietly return to Free — nothing is deleted. The refund policy is linked in the site footer; genuine failures (double payment, activation glitch) are refunded by support.

faq.q: Can I pay for a friend’s account?
faq.a: Premium binds to the Telegram account that activates it. To gift Premium, have them open the Premium menu and pay there, or transfer Stars — the bot cannot attach Premium to a different account after payment.

faq.q: Will Premium renew automatically?
faq.a: The monthly Stars plan renews automatically until cancelled. Prepaid 3-month, 6-month, and yearly plans never auto-renew — when one ends, limits revert to Free and you can extend any time from the Premium menu.

qa_which_plan.title: Free vs Premium: Which Fast Scheduler Plan Fits Your Channel?
qa_which_plan.desc: A decision guide, not a feature dump: how posting volume, channel count, video weight and backup needs map to the right plan — with the exact numbers.
qa_which_plan.content:
Feature tables tell you what differs; this tells you when it matters. Four questions decide the plan.

1. How many channels do you run?

One channel works great on Free ({channels_free} channel, {bots_free} sender bot). Two or three channels — or plans to get there — is the cleanest Premium trigger: Premium pairs {channels_prem} channels with {bots_prem} sender bots from one account.

2. How much do you post?

Multiply daily posts by 30. Under ~90 sends/month, Free's {monthly_sent_free}-per-channel cap rarely bites. A 3+/day cadence, or channels where every send counts (news, trading, drops), wants Premium's unlimited sends and queue.

3. Is your content video-heavy?

Free uploads top out at {max_media_free} with video at {videos_msg_free}, no video in Media Storage, and stronger compression. If your posts live on video, Premium's {max_media_prem} uploads, {videos_msg_prem} video, and video-in-storage are not a luxury — they are the workflow.

4. Do you need backups, exports or signatures?

The Export & Backup toolkit (.fsback archives, JSON/CSV exports) and auto-signatures are Premium-only. If the queue is your business — client channels, monetized content — backups stop being optional the first time you restructure a month of posts.

The short version

  • Stay Free if: one channel, ≤3 posts/day, text-and-photo content, no archive needs.
  • Go Premium if: 2–3 channels, 3+ posts/day, video content, recurring automation beyond one rule, or you want backups and signatures.
  • Either way: you can start Free and upgrade the moment a limit touches you — nothing you built on Free breaks when Premium ends.

faq.q: Can I try Premium and go back to Free?
faq.a: Yes. On expiry, limits revert to Free and nothing is deleted — disconnect extra channels if you keep more than one, and the first recurring rule keeps running.

faq.q: Does Premium change how fast posts send?
faq.a: Send speed is the same — Telegram delivery does not differ by plan. Premium removes quantity limits and media compression, not latency.

qa_post_not_sent.title: Scheduled Message Didn’t Post? The 6 Real Causes, In Order of Likelihood
qa_post_not_sent.desc: A ranked troubleshooting checklist for missed Telegram posts: sender bot admin rights, revoked tokens, permissions, channel changes, rate limits and the monthly cap.
qa_post_not_sent.content:
When a post misses its slot, the cause is almost always in the delivery chain — the schedule itself is the least likely suspect. Work this list top to bottom; each item fixes the majority of cases.

1. The sender bot lost its admin seat

Someone cleaned up admins and removed your sender bot. Check Manage Channel → Administrators: your sender bot must be there with Post Messages. Re-add it, and the queue resumes.

2. The token was revoked or replaced

A /revoke in @BotFather kills the old token everywhere instantly. If the bot shows the sender as disconnected, open Bots → 🔁 Replace Token under the bot and paste the fresh token.

3. Permissions were narrowed

Admin exists but without Post Messages — a silent killer after permission tightening. Open the admin entry and re-enable posting.

4. The channel changed identity

Username changed or the channel was converted — the old link no longer resolves. Reconnect the channel; schedules are kept.

5. Telegram rate limits on bursts
