Telegram throttles aggressive posting bursts channel-wide. If several posts fire close together and one fails, it is usually this. Space posts by minutes, not seconds — the scheduler already does, but third-party bots added to the channel can collide with it.

6. The monthly send cap (Free)

On Free, sends pause at {monthly_sent_free} per channel per month until the 1st. The bot warns you before the cap; /stats shows the counter. Premium lifts the cap entirely.

Fastest diagnosis

Send /stats (status of everything) and check the sender-bot status screen. Still mysterious? /feedback with the channel and the missed time — support can see delivery attempts and will tell you exactly which step failed.

faq.q: Will missed posts send later automatically?
faq.a: A post that failed delivery is marked failed, not silently retried forever. Fix the underlying cause, then delete it and schedule it again.

faq.q: How do I know if it was the monthly cap?
faq.a: The bot notifies you at the cap, and /stats shows monthly usage per channel. If neither shows the cap, it was delivery-side — start the checklist from the top.

qa_signature_guide.title: How to Add an Automatic Signature to Every Telegram Post
qa_signature_guide.desc: Set up a Premium auto-signature — credit line, promo, or hashtags — appended to every post of a channel, with formatting, per-channel control, and clean removal.
qa_signature_guide.content:
A signature is the footer that appears under every post in a channel: credit, CTA, hashtags, promo. Set it once in Fast Scheduler and every scheduled message carries it — you stop copy-pasting “@yourchannel” to the end of everything.

Setting it up

  • 1. Open Signature via /signature (or tap 📝 Signature on the review screen). Premium feature.
  • 2. Pick the channel — signatures are per channel, so your main channel can carry a promo while the announcements channel stays clean.
  • 3. Send the text. Formatting works: bold, italic, links, even emoji-free minimalism if that is your style.

From the next send onward, the signature is appended to every post in that channel. Existing scheduled posts pick it up automatically at send time — no need to reschedule anything.

What belongs in a good signature

  • The channel handle — the classic “@yourchannel” line, since forwarded copies keep the credit.
  • One action — “Reply to buy”, “Details: link”. A signature with three CTAs has zero.
  • Hashtags for navigation — if the channel uses tag-indexing, the signature is the perfect place for the constant ones.

Changing and removing

The same menu edits or clears the signature; clearing stops appending immediately (again, applied at send time, so posts already published keep their footer — that is a feature, not a bug). Per-channel control means experimenting is cheap.

faq.q: Can I use different signatures for different channels?
faq.a: Yes — signatures are configured per channel. Each connected channel gets its own text (or none).

faq.q: Does the signature count toward the message length?
faq.a: It is part of the final message text, so extremely long signatures can hit Telegram’s 4096-character limit on top of long posts. Short signatures are better anyway.

qa_media_storage_guide.title: What Is Media Storage and How Do You Use It Without Losing Your Mind?
qa_media_storage_guide.desc: Media Storage explained: boxes, saved photos/videos/documents, reusing assets across scheduled posts, storage limits on Free vs Premium, and cleanup workflow.
qa_media_storage_guide.content:
Media Storage is your in-bot asset library: save a photo, video, or document once, then reuse it in any scheduled post without re-uploading. If you repost evergreen content or reuse brand imagery, this is the feature that saves the most time per week.

Boxes: folders with a purpose

Assets live in boxes — named containers like “Brand”, “Memes”, “Product shots”. Free gets {storage_count_free} box with {storage_items_free} items (no video in storage); Premium gets {storage_count_prem} boxes × {storage_items_prem} items with video support. Boxes keep the picker fast and your library mentally organized — one box per campaign is a good default.

Saving and reusing

  • Save: forward or upload media to the storage, or save straight from a scheduled message you are composing.
  • Reuse: while scheduling, open the storage instead of attaching a file — pick the asset, done. Telegram file references are reused, so nothing is re-uploaded and quality is not recompressed per post.
  • Organize: move items between boxes, rename, delete.

The limits that actually matter

  • Item count — the {storage_items_free}-item Free box fills fast with albums; delete stale assets or upgrade.
  • Video on Free — storage refuses video on Free; schedule videos directly instead, or move to Premium for video-in-storage.
  • Size — same upload caps as messages: {max_media_free} on Free, {max_media_prem} on Premium.

A cleanup cadence that works

Once a month: open each box, delete anything unused in 60 days, archive campaign boxes by renaming with a date prefix. Two minutes, and the picker stays a joy instead of an archaeology dig.

faq.q: Does deleting a media item break scheduled posts using it?
faq.a: Posts keep working — a scheduled message holds its own reference to the media. Deleting from storage only removes it from the library for future posts.

faq.q: Can I share a box with another admin?
faq.a: Storage is per account. To share assets, export them as part of a backup or send the files directly — the other account saves them into their own storage.

qa_recurring_guide.title: How to Automate Recurring Posts in Telegram (Daily Digests, Weekly Roundups)
qa_recurring_guide.desc: Recurring rules done right: every supported interval, expiry behavior, combining recurrences with signatures, and real channel patterns that run themselves.
qa_recurring_guide.content:
Anything your channel repeats should never be scheduled by hand twice. Recurring rules encode the pattern once — “daily at 9:00”, “every Monday 18:30”, “every 6 hours” — and the bot keeps generating posts on time, forever (or until the rule expires).

Creating a rule

  • 1. Tap 🔄 Recurring Messages in the bot (or send /recurring) and follow the flow.
  • 2. Compose the message — text, media, the works — exactly like a normal post.
  • 3. Pick the pattern: daily, weekly (with weekday picker), or custom interval.
  • 4. Set the time in the channel's time zone and confirm.

The rule's future posts expand in the Calendar like any others, and the rule itself is listed with your recurring messages — so there is always a truthful picture of what will publish.

Expiry — the part people forget

On Free, the single recurring rule runs for {recurring_expiry_days} days, then expires with a notice — create a new rule to continue. It is the anti-zombie mechanism: dead rules can't silently post forever. Premium rules never expire, and you can run unlimited rules — one per content type is the usual pattern.

Patterns that work in real channels

  • Daily digest — a template message (“Top 3 of the day”) with the signature carrying credit; edit the rule weekly, not daily.
  • Weekly roundup — Monday 9:00 rule; combine with the calendar to dodge holidays.
  • Scheduled reminders — every-6-hours service posts for community managers; Premium's unlimited rules shine here.

Editing and stopping

Rules are editable — change text, time, or pattern, and future instances follow. Pause or delete when a campaign ends. Deleting a rule never deletes already-posted messages.

faq.q: Why did my recurring rule stop working?
faq.a: On Free, rules expire after 365 days and you get an expiry notice — create a new rule to continue. Premium rules never expire. Also check the sender bot is still admin — a failed delivery stops the chain.

faq.q: Can two rules post at the same time?
faq.a: Yes, and they will — in the order created. If they are too close together, Telegram may throttle the burst; space rules by a few minutes.

qa_bot_management.title: How to Manage Your Sender Bots: Rotate, Rename, and Keep Them Healthy
qa_bot_management.desc: Day-to-day sender bot management: checking status, rotating a compromised token, renaming the public face of your bot, one-bot-per-channel hygiene, and removal.
qa_bot_management.content:
Your sender bot is the public face of every post, so a little hygiene goes a long way. Everything below lives in Sender Bots (or /bots) in Fast Scheduler.

Check status before you check anything else

The bots screen shows each bot's connection state and which channels it serves. If a send ever fails, this is the first screen: a bot showing disconnected means a revoked token or a BotFather change — fix it there, not in the schedule.

Rotating a token (the right way)

  • 1. @BotFather → /mybots → your bot → Revoke current token.
  • 2. Copy the new token.
  • 3. Fast Scheduler → Bots → 🔁 Replace Token under the bot → paste.

The swap is instant and schedules keep running. Do it the other way around (revoke and forget) and every send fails until you paste the new token.

Rename = rebrand

A bot's public name and avatar come from @BotFather (/setname, /setuserpic) — change them there and every future post instantly carries the new look. No re-pairing needed; Fast Scheduler stores the token, not the cosmetics.

Fleet hygiene

  • One bot per channel keeps branding separate and failures isolated (Premium: up to {bots_prem} bots).
  • Remove bots you no longer use — removal deletes the token from storage; the bot account itself lives on in BotFather.
  • After any BotFather change, glance at the status screen once — 10 seconds that prevent a silent failed-post day.

faq.q: Can I use the same bot for multiple channels?
faq.a: Yes — a sender bot can serve several of your channels. Separate bots per channel remain the cleaner default for branding and debugging.

faq.q: I deleted a bot in BotFather. What happens in Fast Scheduler?
faq.a: Its sends fail with an invalid-token error and the status screen shows it disconnected. Remove the bot from Sender Bots and pair a replacement.

qa_private_channel_connect.title: How Do I Connect a Private Telegram Channel to Fast Scheduler?
qa_private_channel_connect.desc: Private Telegram channels work with Fast Scheduler too. Four ways to connect one — @username, forwarding a post, an invite link, or the -100 ID.
qa_private_channel_connect.content:
Private channels are fully supported — the bot never needs to be able to search your channel, it only needs to be inside it as an admin. There are four accepted ways to point Fast Scheduler at a private channel, and at least one of them will take you under a minute.

Before you start: give the bots admin rights

  • Open your private channel → Administrators → Add Admin.
  • Add @FastSchedulerBot with the Post Messages permission. That single permission is enough to schedule and publish.
  • Then, inside Fast Scheduler, pair a sender bot and make it an admin of the same channel. This step is mandatory: every scheduled post is published through your sender bot, never through the main bot, so nothing in the scheduling flow unlocks until each connected channel has one.

Four ways to connect the channel

Open the bot → Channels → Connect Channel, then send whichever of these is easiest for you:

  • @username — private channels have no @username, so this one is mostly for public channels.
  • Forward any post from the channel to the bot. This is the fastest way for private channels: open the channel, long-press any message, Forward → Fast Scheduler Bot. The bot reads the source channel from the forward.
  • An invite link — copy Invite Link from the channel menu and paste it into the chat.
  • The channel ID — the numeric -100… identifier (e.g. -1001234567890) if you know it from another tool.

Why the invite-link and forward methods are equivalent

Both simply resolve your private channel to its internal ID. Fast Scheduler stores that ID plus your admin status; the channel’s privacy settings never matter again after the connection is made. You can rename the channel, change its link, or toggle “slow mode” — the connection survives all of it.

If connecting fails

  • Bot is not an admin — re-check step one; the permission check runs live against Telegram.
  • Invite link revoked or set to “join request” — regenerate the link, or forward a post instead.
  • You are not the owner — the connector must hold admin rights in the channel under the account that talks to the bot.

Free plan: {channels_free} channel. Premium raises this to {channels_prem}, each with its own sender bot, time zone and statistics.

faq.q: Can Fast Scheduler post to a private channel?
faq.a: Yes. Private channels are connected by forwarding a post from the channel, pasting an invite link, or sending the -100 channel ID. The channel being private does not affect scheduling in any way.

faq.q: Does the sender bot also need admin rights in a private channel?
faq.a: Yes. The main bot needs Post Messages to verify and manage, and your sender bot needs Post Messages because it is the account that actually publishes every scheduled post.

faq.q: How many channels can I connect on the Free plan?
faq.a: Free includes {channels_free} channel with {monthly_sent_free} sent messages per month. Premium raises the limit to {channels_prem} channels with unlimited sends.

qa_refund_how.title: How Do I Get a Refund on My Fast Scheduler Premium Purchase?
qa_refund_how.desc: Paid with Telegram Stars and changed your mind? Here is exactly how to request a refund: the email, what to include, the 30-day window and processing times.
qa_refund_how.content:
Refunds are handled personally, not by a faceless form. If a purchase went wrong — a double charge, an accidental renewal, Premium that never activated — you write one email and a human sorts it out. Here is the whole procedure, step by step.

What to send

Email fastschedulebot@gmail.com with three things:

  • Your transaction ID — Telegram shows it in the Stars payment confirmation and in Settings → Payments.
  • Your Telegram username (or user ID) so the purchase can be matched to your account.
  • The reason — one honest sentence is enough, plus the purchase date and the account or email used, where applicable.

The 30-day window and what happens next

Refund requests are accepted within 30 days of the charge. Requests are acknowledged within 7 business days, and approved refunds are returned through the original payment method — for Telegram Stars that means back to your Stars balance. Refunds are discretionary rather than guaranteed for every situation, which is exactly why a short, honest reason helps: accidental purchases and technical failures the team could not fix are the classic approved cases.

Cancelling so you are not charged again

Monthly Stars plans renew automatically until cancelled. You cancel inside the bot: open /premium → ❌ Cancel Premium. Cancelling stops future billing; the period you already paid for stays active until its end date, and Premium switches off at that boundary rather than mid-plan. The 3-month, 6-month and yearly packs are one-time purchases — they simply expire and never auto-charge.

What not to do: chargebacks

Opening a card or Apple/Google chargeback instead of emailing is treated as abuse: the account loses Premium immediately and the subscription fee is forfeited. Emailing first is always faster — most refund conversations end within a couple of messages.

One more nuance: deleting your data or stopping use of the bot does not automatically refund anything, so if you want both, request the refund before asking for account deletion.

faq.q: How long does a Fast Scheduler refund take?
faq.a: Requests are acknowledged within 7 business days. Once approved, Stars refunds return to your Telegram Stars balance; the total time depends on Telegram, typically a few days.

faq.q: Can I cancel Premium and keep it until the period ends?
faq.a: Yes. Cancelling via /premium stops auto-renewal, and Premium stays active until the end of the paid period. Downgrade happens at that boundary, not immediately.

faq.q: I was charged twice. What do I do?
faq.a: Email fastschedulebot@gmail.com with both transaction IDs and your Telegram username. Duplicate charges are the clearest refund case and are resolved quickly.

qa_timezone_wrong_time.title: Why Was My Scheduled Telegram Post Published at the Wrong Time?
qa_timezone_wrong_time.desc: A post set for 9:00 went out at 6:00 or 12:00? The cause is almost always a time-zone mismatch. Here is how Fast Scheduler resolves times and how to fix it.
qa_timezone_wrong_time.content:
When a scheduled message fires at an unexpected hour, the clock itself is almost never wrong — the time zone used to interpret “9:00” is. Fast Scheduler resolves every time through two settings, and a mismatch between them explains nearly every “wrong time” report.

The two clocks: user time zone and channel time zone

  • Your user time zone — set once via /timezone and used whenever you type a time into the scheduling conversation.
  • Each channel’s own time zone — set per channel, because the audience that reads the channel may live in a different zone than you do. Schedules for that channel are interpreted in the channel’s zone.

If your user zone says UTC+3 but the channel zone says UTC+0, a message you schedule for 9:00 is stored as 9:00 channel time — and lands six hours earlier than you visually expected. Check both: /timezone for yourself, and the channel settings inside the bot for the channel.

Daylight saving time

Zones with DST shift by one hour twice a year. Fast Scheduler stores schedules in absolute terms, so a post that crossed a DST boundary can appear to “move” by an hour. If you live in a DST zone and noticed the shift right after the clocks changed, re-check the channel’s zone — picking a zone like Europe/Berlin (which follows DST rules) versus a fixed UTC offset produces different results across the year.

Quick diagnosis checklist

  • Off by a round number of hours (3, 4, 6…) → time-zone mismatch; fix the channel time zone or your user zone.
  • Off by exactly one hour right after late March / late October → DST; confirm the zone uses the right convention.
  • AM/PM confusion — schedule with the 24-hour clock (14:00, not 2:00) to remove ambiguity entirely.
  • Around midnight — double-check you scheduled the day you meant; the date picker always shows the resolved local date and time for final confirmation before saving.

One more tip: the confirmation screen before saving shows the exact send time. Reading that single line — not the input you typed — is the ground truth for when the post will fire.

faq.q: Does each Telegram channel have its own time zone in Fast Scheduler?
faq.a: Yes. Every channel carries its own time zone, and schedules for that channel are interpreted in the channel zone. Your personal /timezone setting applies to how you enter times while chatting with the bot.

faq.q: How do I change the time zone of a channel?
faq.a: Open the bot, go to the channel settings, and set its time zone there. Existing scheduled messages keep their stored times, so new schedules pick up the change immediately.

qa_stats_views.title: How Can I See Views, Reactions and Comments on My Telegram Channel Posts?
qa_stats_views.desc: Fast Scheduler tracks views, comments and reactions for every post it publishes — with per-channel dashboards and Premium leaderboards of your top content.
qa_stats_views.content:
Telegram shows view counts under every channel post, but it never shows you trends: which topics overperform, what time of day your audience actually reads, which posts collected the most reactions. Fast Scheduler records the metrics of every post it publishes and turns them into dashboards you can browse in seconds.

Where the numbers live

Open Statistics on the bot’s main menu (page 2) or send /stats. You get:

  • Usage totals — lifetime messages sent, messages sent today, and how many schedules and recurring messages are currently active.
  • Per-channel dashboards — for every connected channel: average views, comments and reactions per post, plus the top reactions your audience uses.
  • Leaderboards (Premium) — your top posts ranked by the metric you pick: Views, Comments, Reactions or Top Commenters. Each board shows 10 entries per page and can be filtered by period (day, week, month, year or all time).

What is counted — and what is not

Statistics are recorded when Fast Scheduler publishes a post and Telegram reports back the post’s metrics. Manually posted content that never passed through the bot is deliberately excluded, so the numbers describe your scheduled content honestly. Comments made in the discussion group under a channel post are picked up too, which is what powers the Comments metric and the Top Commenters board.

Three ways to actually use this

  • Find your format. Sort by Views for a month: if the top five posts share a pattern (length, media type, topic), schedule more of it.
  • Time your channel. Compare identical formats posted at different hours, then move recurring messages toward the winning window — the best posting times guide below has the general playbook.
  • Watch reactions, not just views. Views measure reach; reactions and comments measure resonance. A post with half the views but double the reaction rate is usually the better template.

faq.q: Does Fast Scheduler track posts I publish manually?
faq.a: No. Only posts published through Fast Scheduler are recorded, which keeps your dashboards focused on your scheduled content strategy.

faq.q: Are statistics leaderboards free?
faq.a: Per-channel averages and usage totals are available to everyone. Leaderboards that rank your top posts by views, comments or reactions are part of Premium.

faq.q: What metrics can leaderboards rank by?
faq.a: Views, comments, reactions and top commenters — each filterable by day, week, month, year or all time, with up to 50 posts per page.

qa_media_types.title: What Types of Content Can You Schedule With Fast Scheduler?
qa_media_types.desc: Photos, videos, GIFs, voice messages, stickers, polls, documents, locations — every media type Fast Scheduler can schedule to a Telegram channel.
qa_media_types.content:
A scheduling bot is only as good as the content it can carry. Fast Scheduler handles the full Telegram media palette, so your editorial plans never have to shrink to fit the tool.

Everything you can attach to a scheduled post

  • Photos — compressed automatically for fast delivery without visible quality loss.
  • Videos — including size limits that scale with your plan ({videos_msg_free} on Free, {videos_msg_prem} on Premium).
  • Video notes (round videos) and voice messages.
  • Audio files — full tracks with cover art preserved.
  • Documents — PDFs, archives, anything Telegram accepts.
  • Animations — GIFs and MP4 loops.
  • Stickers — from any of your packs.
  • Polls and quizzes — scheduled like any other post.
  • Locations and venues — supported for per-post content.

Albums and media groups

Multiple photos or videos sent together are scheduled as one album and publish as a single media group — exactly how your followers expect it. You can also build a randomized pool: attach a mix of photos, videos, documents or any files and let the scheduler pick one per send, which is perfect for daily wallpaper or quote channels where variety matters.

Text always travels with media

Captions keep their formatting (bold, italic, links, spoilers) and your configured signature is appended to media posts as well. Inline URL buttons attach to media posts too, so a “Read more” button under a photo works out of the box.

Limits that matter

  • Uploads: up to {max_media_free} on Free, {max_media_prem} on Premium.
  • Videos: {videos_msg_free} on Free, {videos_msg_prem} on Premium.
  • Media Storage boxes: {storage_count_free} box with {storage_items_free} items on Free — Premium multiplies both, so reusable assets live in the bot instead of your camera roll.

Anything Telegram itself refuses (for example, a corrupted file) is rejected at scheduling time with a clear message — never discovered silently on the day of publishing.

faq.q: Can I schedule Telegram polls with Fast Scheduler?
faq.a: Yes. Polls and quizzes are scheduled like any other message and publish through your sender bot at the set time.

faq.q: Can I schedule an album of photos?
faq.a: Yes. Photos and videos sent together are scheduled as one media group. You can also attach a pool of mixed files and let the scheduler pick one randomly per send.

faq.q: What is the maximum video size for scheduled messages?
faq.a: Videos {videos_msg_free} on the Free plan and {videos_msg_prem} with Premium, in line with Telegram bots own upload limits.

qa_delete_data.title: How Do I Delete My Fast Scheduler Account and All My Data?
qa_delete_data.desc: Want everything removed? Here is how account deletion works, what exactly gets erased, why you should export a backup first, and what happens on Telegram side.
qa_delete_data.content:
You can leave Fast Scheduler completely — no subscriptions to cancel by email, no dark patterns, no “are you sure” maze. One message, and everything tied to your Telegram account is erased.

How to request deletion

Contact @MaximalXP in Telegram and ask to delete your account. Deletion is permanent and covers all data associated with your user ID: scheduled and recurring messages, media storage, sender-bot tokens, channel connections, settings, statistics and referral records.

Export first — deletion has no undo

Before deleting, create a backup with /backup (a Premium toolkit) or export individual lists, so your content plan survives the account. Once deletion runs, there is no recovery path — the data no longer exists to restore.

What happens on Telegram’s side

  • Your sender bots keep existing in @BotFather — they are your bots, created with your account. If you want them gone too, revoke or delete them there after deletion. Revoke first if you plan to keep using them elsewhere.
  • The bot loses admin rights relevance immediately, but you can also remove @FastSchedulerBot and your sender bot from your channels’ admin lists yourself — a good hygiene step that takes ten seconds per channel.
  • Already-published posts stay in your channel, of course — deletion cannot rewrite history.

How long data is kept normally

While you are an active user, every category of data is kept only while it is useful: schedules until they are deleted or sent, bot tokens until you disconnect the bot, and account records until you delete the account. The Privacy Policy’s retention table lists each category with its exact lifetime.

faq.q: Who do I contact to delete my Fast Scheduler account?
faq.a: Message @MaximalXP on Telegram and request account deletion. The deletion is permanent and removes all data linked to your Telegram ID.

faq.q: Can I delete everything but keep the bot?
faq.a: Yes — you can delete individual schedules, media and sender bots from inside the bot without deleting your account. Full deletion is only for leaving the service entirely.

faq.q: Should I export a backup before deleting?
faq.a: Definitely. After deletion there is no way to restore anything, so create a backup with /backup first if there is any chance you will return.

qa_setdate_bulk.title: How Do I Schedule Many Telegram Posts at Once? (Bulk Scheduling with SetDate)
qa_setdate_bulk.desc: Queue dozens of channel posts in minutes: prepare them in the SetDate companion bot, pick dates and times, and import everything into Fast Scheduler in one click.
qa_setdate_bulk.content:
Scheduling one post is quick. Scheduling thirty — a week of content for a news channel, a course drip, a product launch sequence — needs a different tool: SetDate, the companion bot built for exactly this.

The five-minute bulk workflow

  • 1. Open SetDate. Open @SetDate_bot directly — or tap 📅 Use SetDate Bot whenever Fast Scheduler suggests it.
  • 2. Feed it content. Send your messages one after another — text, photos, videos, anything you would schedule normally.
  • 3. Choose a start date and how many posts should go out per day.
  • 4. Define posting times — for example 09:00, 14:00 and 18:00 — and SetDate distributes your messages across that grid.
  • 5. Send the batch back. One tap and every message appears in Fast Scheduler as a normal scheduled post, fully editable afterwards.

Why this beats scheduling by hand

  • One sitting instead of thirty. You write all content while you are in the writing mood, then let the grid place it.
  • Perfect for recurring formats. A daily tip at 10:00 for the next two weeks is two fields in SetDate, not fourteen conversations.
  • Everything stays editable. After import, each post is a regular scheduled message — search it, edit it, delete it, or move it in the calendar.

Bulk for repeated content: recurring messages

If the same message should repeat — a weekly digest, a daily reminder — you do not need bulk import at all: create a recurring message once and it reschedules itself. Free plans run {recurring_free} recurring message; Premium removes the cap ({recurring_prem}) and its rules never expire.

Tip: before importing a large batch, glance at your channel’s time zone (see the time-zone guide) so the grid lands on the hours you actually meant.

faq.q: What is the SetDate bot?
faq.a: SetDate is Fast Scheduler’s companion bot for bulk scheduling: you prepare many messages there, choose a start date and daily posting times, and import them all into Fast Scheduler in one click.

faq.q: Can I edit posts after bulk import?
faq.a: Yes. Imported messages become ordinary scheduled messages — open the Message List or calendar and edit, move or delete any of them individually.

faq.q: How many posts can I import at once?
faq.a: Imported messages count against your scheduled-message limit ({scheduled_free} pending on Free, unlimited on Premium), so a batch that fits your queue can be imported in one go.

tg_channel_vs_group.title: Telegram Channel vs Group: What Is the Difference and Which One Do You Need?
tg_channel_vs_group.desc: Channels broadcast, groups converse. A practical comparison for creators — and how Fast Scheduler fits each, including discussion-group comments.
tg_channel_vs_group.content:
New Telegram creators constantly mix these up, and picking wrong shapes everything after it — including how you schedule. Here is the short, practical version.

The one-line difference

A channel is a megaphone: only admins publish, everyone else reads. A group is a round table: every member can post and reply. A channel can have a linked discussion group, which adds a comment thread under every channel post — the best of both worlds.

Choose a channel when…

  • You publish content to an audience: news, deals, tutorials, drops.
  • You want a clean feed readers can scroll without chatter.
  • You care about per-post view counts — channels show them, groups do not.

Choose a group when…

  • Conversation is the product: support, community, coordination.
  • You want members to see each other and reply freely.

The classic combo

Most serious projects end up with both: a channel for polished posts, plus a linked discussion group for the conversation under them. Telegram links them in the channel settings; from then on every channel post automatically gets a comment thread.

Where Fast Scheduler fits

Fast Scheduler publishes to channels — that is where scheduled broadcast content belongs. Because it also tracks the discussion-group comments under the posts it publishes, your statistics cover the conversational side too: average comments per post and Top Commenters leaderboards work with the combo setup out of the box. The practical recipe: plan and queue polished posts in the channel, and let the linked group absorb the discussion they spark.

faq.q: Can Fast Scheduler post to groups?
faq.a: Fast Scheduler schedules to channels, which is the broadcast use case it is built for. For community discussion, create a channel with a linked discussion group — comments there are tracked in your statistics.

faq.q: What is a discussion group in Telegram?
faq.a: A group linked to your channel in channel settings. Every channel post gets a comment thread in that group, giving readers a place to reply without polluting the channel feed.

qa_formatting.title: How Do I Format Telegram Posts? (Bold, Italic, Links, Spoilers and Buttons)
qa_formatting.desc: Everything about formatting scheduled Telegram posts: entities preserved from your drafts, spoiler markup, custom emoji, and inline URL buttons with simple syntax.
qa_formatting.content:
Formatting is what separates a channel that looks professional from one that looks like a group chat. Fast Scheduler keeps every bit of it intact between scheduling and publishing.

Rich text survives the whole pipeline

Write a message anywhere — bold headlines, italic asides, underlined warnings, struck-through corrections, monospace code — and schedule it. Formatting is stored as Telegram entities, not flat text, so what publishes is pixel-identical to what you wrote: no mangled asterisks, no lost links, no broken emoji.

Spoilers

Wrap part of the text in spoiler markup and it publishes as a real Telegram spoiler — blurred until a reader taps it. Perfect for giveaways, answers, and sensitive details. The bot validates spoiler markup while you type, so unclosed pairs are caught at scheduling time, not in front of your audience.

Inline URL buttons

Add tappable buttons to any post with one syntax: [Button Text](https://example.com). Use them for call-to-action links — “Read the guide”, “Buy now”, “Join the chat”. Buttons attach to text posts and to media posts alike. Keep button labels short (two or three words read best) and test one post before scheduling a whole campaign.

Custom emoji

Premium Telegram emoji in your drafts are preserved on publish, so your brand’s custom smileys do not degrade into defaults.

Signatures: formatting that stamps itself

Configure a signature once — a footer with your links, hashtags or contact — and every scheduled post carries it automatically, on text and media alike. Signatures keep their own formatting, and you can override the signature per post when a particular message should go out clean.

A checklist for polished posts

  • One bold hook line first — most readers see only it in notifications.
  • Links as buttons where possible; they out-click inline links.
  • Spoilers for anything the reader should opt into.
  • A signature so every post quietly advertises your next channel.

faq.q: Does Telegram formatting survive scheduling in Fast Scheduler?
faq.a: Yes. Bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, code, links, spoilers and custom emoji are stored as Telegram entities and publish exactly as written.

faq.q: How do I add buttons to a scheduled Telegram post?
faq.a: Use the syntax [Button Text](https://your-link.com) in the message. The bot converts it into a tappable inline URL button on the published post.

faq.q: Can every scheduled post have an automatic signature?
faq.a: Yes. Create a signature once and it is appended to every scheduled and recurring post automatically, keeping its own formatting. Individual posts can override it.

qa_what_is_fast_scheduler.title: What Is Fast Scheduler? The Telegram Post Scheduling Bot Explained
qa_what_is_fast_scheduler.desc: Fast Scheduler is a Telegram bot that schedules and auto-publishes posts to your channels: queues, recurring messages, sender bots, statistics and backups. Here is the full picture.
qa_what_is_fast_scheduler.content:
Fast Scheduler (@FastSchedulerBot) is a Telegram bot that plans and publishes posts to your channels on a schedule — the missing native feature Telegram never shipped properly. You write content when inspiration strikes; the bot delivers it at the hour your audience actually reads.

How it works in three roles

  • The main bot (@FastSchedulerBot) is your control room: every conversation, every schedule, every statistic happens here.
  • Your channel — connect it once by making the bots admins; the bot verifies rights and tracks it from then on.
  • A sender bot — a small bot of your own (created in @BotFather in two minutes) that actually publishes the posts, so your channel’s byline is your brand, not ours. Connecting one is required: scheduling unlocks only after each channel has a sender bot.

What you can do with it

  • Schedule anything — text, photos, videos, GIFs, voice, stickers, documents, polls, albums, with full formatting, spoilers and URL buttons.
  • Recurring messages — a post that repeats daily, weekly or on custom patterns without re-scheduling.
  • Bulk import — prepare a week of content in the SetDate companion bot and import it in one click.
  • Statistics — views, comments and reactions per channel, with leaderboards of your top posts.
  • Team features — admin permissions, shared channel limits, ownership transfer with confirmation phrases.
  • Backups & export — encrypted .fspback backups, JSON/CSV exports, migration between accounts.

Free vs Premium, honestly

  • Free: {channels_free} channel and sender bot, {scheduled_free} pending scheduled messages, {monthly_sent_free} sends per channel per month, {recurring_free} recurring message — enough to run one channel seriously.
  • Premium ({premium_monthly}/mo or {premium_yearly}/yr): {channels_prem} channels and sender bots, unlimited scheduled queue, unlimited sends, unlimited recurring messages, bigger uploads ({max_media_prem}), leaderboards, backups, inline buttons and more.

Who it is for

News channels that publish on rhythm, creators who batch their week in one sitting, shops running drops at precise hours, and community managers who share channels with a team. If you have ever set a 3 a.m. alarm to post manually — this bot is the cure.

Start here: open @FastSchedulerBot, press Start, connect your channel, pair a sender bot, and schedule your first post before your coffee cools.

faq.q: Is Fast Scheduler free?
faq.a: Yes — the Free plan runs one channel with {scheduled_free} pending scheduled messages and {monthly_sent_free} sends per channel per month, forever. Premium at {premium_monthly}/mo lifts every cap and adds statistics leaderboards, backups and bigger uploads.

faq.q: Why does Fast Scheduler need a sender bot?
faq.a: Your sender bot publishes the posts, so your channel’s byline is your own brand instead of a third-party bot. It is created by you in @BotFather and connected in two minutes.

faq.q: Can Fast Scheduler send messages to a Telegram channel automatically?
faq.a: Yes. That is its core purpose: scheduled messages publish automatically at their set time through your sender bot, including media, formatting and buttons.

extrasec_reach-1000-subscribers-telegram.content:
The seeding loop, step by step

The first hundred subscribers almost never come from promotion — they come from seeding: deliberately placing your channel in front of small, warm audiences until a base exists that can grow on its own. The loop looks like this:

  1. List every community you already belong to. Work chats, university groups, gaming clans, a neighborhood chat, a hobby forum. Most people can name ten without trying. These are your seeding spots.
  2. Give before you link. In each community, spend a week being useful: answer questions, share things with no signature. People check the profile of anyone who posts something good — that's why your channel link lives in your bio, not in your messages.
  3. Post the artifact, not the ad. When the channel has something genuinely valuable — a checklist, a dataset, a teardown — share the artifact itself in the community where it's relevant. One good artifact outperforms twenty "subscribe to my channel" messages, which get you banned from admins instead.
  4. Close the loop with comments. When someone joins from a seed and comments, reply fast and personally. The first hundred should each feel like they were let into something.

Run the loop for a month and measure honestly: if ten communities produced forty subscribers, you know your per-seed conversion — and whether the content or the seeding spots need to change before you scale the effort.

Swap etiquette that gets you a second swap

Swaps — you post for me, I post for you — are the standard growth currency from roughly 300 subscribers upward. Most swap requests get ignored not because the channel is small, but because the request is lazy. The etiquette that gets yeses:

  • Match by ERR, not size. A 2,000-subscriber channel with 40% view rates delivers more real eyeballs than a 10,000 channel at 8%. Quote your average views of the last ten posts, never the subscriber count.
  • Write the promo post for them. Include the post, the link, and one line of context on why your audience would care. The fewer decisions your partner has to make, the faster the deal closes.
  • Post at your best hour and expect the same. A swap buried at 3 a.m. is wasted on both sides; agree on the slot explicitly.
  • Send a screenshot of the results afterward. Views, taps, joins. Partners re-swap with channels that report; they ghost the ones that don't.

A practical cadence: two swaps per week at the same tier, for six weeks, beats any paid promo at this stage — it compounds, because every swap partner exposes you to another admin who now knows your channel exists.

extrasec_telegram-channel-ideas.content:
Idea 1 — The job board that answers one question

Take "jobs channel" and cut it until only one question remains. Not "remote jobs" — "remote React jobs, Europe, salary listed, posted the day they appear." That description answers the three things every job-seeker asks: is it for me, is it real, how old is it. The mechanics that make this class of channel retain:

  • A fixed format per post. Role, location, salary range, apply link, one line on the company. Predictable format lets readers scan in two seconds and makes the channel feel like infrastructure rather than content.
  • Ruthless freshness. Reposting week-old openings is the fastest way to lose a job-board audience. Date-stamp everything; delete or mark expired entries.
  • A submission funnel. Recruiters will find you once you're consistent — give them a bot or a form. Sourced listings also solve your hardest problem at scale: they're self-replenishing content.
  • The weekly digest. One post per week summarizing the best ten listings. Digests get forwarded to colleagues, and forwards are this niche's growth engine.

Monetization arrives naturally later — featured listings and recruiter promos — but only after the archive of past posts proves you never posted junk. Job boards live and die on trust in the filter.

Idea 2 — The hyperlocal channel (the most underrated class)

National channels compete with media giants; a channel for one district of one city has no competition at all. Hyperlocal is the most defensible niche on Telegram because the moat is physical presence: you know which playground reopened, which pharmacy has the medicine, when the hot water goes off. What retains people:

  • Utility density. A single useful post — road closures this weekend, the school's schedule change — gets forwarded into family chats, which is where the subscribers come from. Parents, in particular, treat a good local channel as a public service.
  • Civic micro-news. Council decisions, utility works, local business openings/closings. Boring individually, indispensable in aggregate.
  • A comments culture that stays civil. Local channels attract strong opinions; a linked discussion group with light moderation keeps the channel readable. This is the one niche where moderation bots pay for themselves first.

The honest difficulty: hyperlocal doesn't scale and doesn't sell to national advertisers. It monetizes through local businesses — a bakery announcement reaches exactly the people who can walk there, which is worth real money to the bakery.

Idea 3 — Build-in-public: the retention machine

A build-in-public channel documents one project — a SaaS, a newsletter, a YouTube channel, even the Telegram channel itself — with real numbers: revenue, costs, mistakes, decisions. It retains better than almost any other format for one structural reason: it's a story with unmade episodes. Subscribers don't stay for the niche; they stay to find out what happens next. What makes it work:

  • Real numbers, including unflattering ones. "MRR: $340, down from $410 — here's what I think happened" builds more trust than any highlight reel. The audience for this format is sophisticated; they can smell curation.
  • A consistent cadence with a structure. A weekly numbers post, plus as-needed decision posts. The fixed slot turns checking the channel into a habit.
  • Decision points, not just milestones. "Should I raise prices? Here's the data, vote in the comments" — participatory moments convert readers into stakeholders, and stakeholders don't unsubscribe.
  • An end condition. Paradoxically, naming the finish line — "until $2,000 MRR or twelve months" — increases retention. Open-ended diaries feel like homework; bounded series feel like a season.

Idea 4 — Micro-lessons: the course hiding in a feed

Teaching channels retain because progress is addictive: each post is a small, completable unit. The format that works isn't essays — it's micro-lessons: one concept, one example, one exercise, under 150 words. A language channel posts five words a day with usage examples; a design channel breaks down one layout choice per post; a finance channel explains one term with a real number. The mechanics worth stealing:

  • Numbered progression. "Lesson 47" in the post header creates collection pressure — people scroll back and read the archive, which is what separates a channel from a feed.
  • Spaced repetition on purpose. Resurface lesson 12's concept inside lesson 40's example. Readers notice the callback and feel rewarded for paying attention.
  • Exercise posts with next-day answers. The answer post drives next-day opens, and comments fill with attempts — engagement the algorithm and other subscribers both reward.
  • A pinned syllabus. One post indexing the whole course, updated as it grows. New arrivals binge; binging is the strongest subscribe signal there is.

Idea 5 — Deals and error-fares: trust is the entire product

Deal channels (gadgets, books, flights, games) have the highest raw engagement of any class — people act on them — and the most fragile trust. One affiliate-padded fake deal and the channel is done. The operators who last treat the filter as the product:

  • Post only deals you'd send to a friend. A simple test that eliminates half the affiliate inventory in any niche. The channel's value is precisely the deals it doesn't post.
  • Show the math. Price history (is this actually a discount?), the retailer, the catch. Deal-savvy readers check camel-price trackers anyway; get ahead of them.
  • Speed windows. Error fares and flash deals expire in hours — the channel needs a posting rhythm fast enough to matter. This is the niche where scheduled batches don't fit, and where a queue you can fire instantly from your phone does.
  • Disclosure discipline. Affiliate links marked, always. Counter-intuitively, marked links convert better in this class, because the audience knows exactly what they're looking at.

extrasec_grow-telegram-channel-from-zero.content:
Weeks 1–2 in detail: what "set up" actually means

The 90-day plan compresses at week level; here's the un-compressed version of the first two weeks, because this is where most channels quietly fail:

  • Write the first ten posts before inviting anyone. Not five — ten. The first visitors scroll the whole wall; a wall with ten substantive posts reads as an institution, one with three reads as an abandoned experiment.
  • Fix the posting slots now. Choose two or three weekly slots based on when your audience is actually on Telegram (evening hours in their timezone, generally), and queue the first two weeks against those slots. Scheduled publishing removes the daily willpower tax, which is the real killer of week three.
  • Set up measurement on day one. Note the baseline: subscribers, views per post. Every scheduler's stats page plus a simple spreadsheet is enough. The plan's weekly decisions depend on having honest numbers from the start, not reconstructed ones later.
  • Seed list of ten places. Written down, with a plan for each. "I'll be useful in X for a week before mentioning anything" is a plan; "promote everywhere" is a wish.

Exit criteria for week two: ten posts published, two weeks queued, baseline recorded, first seeds placed. If any of those slipped, week three's growth work rests on sand — finish the foundation first.

The metrics that actually decide the weekly review

The 90-day plan says "track metrics weekly"; these are the ones worth a spreadsheet row, and what each one tells you:

  • Views-to-subscribers (V/S). Your content quality signal. Healthy small channels run 25–60%. If it slides for three consecutive weeks while subscribers hold, the content has drifted from what joiners expected.
  • Net adds per week, split by source. Seeding, swaps, search, forwards — even a rough attribution tells you which engine to feed. Most channels discover one source produces 80% and starve it by spreading effort evenly.
  • Unsubscribe timing. Joins/leaves attached to specific posts (any decent scheduler shows this). A promo post that reliably triggers leave-waves is costing more than it pays.
  • The forwarding signal. Which posts get forwarded (Telegram shows forward counts). Forwards are the only organic distribution on the platform — double down on whatever earns them.

One number to deliberately ignore: subscriber count as a headline. It's the output of the four metrics above, and staring at it weekly produces exactly the impatient decisions that stall channels.

extrasec_cross-promotion-telegram-swaps.content:
The swap marketplace, mapped

Beyond cold DMs, an actual infrastructure exists for finding swap partners — knowing the map saves weeks:

  • TGStat and Telemetr catalogs are the discovery layer: filter by category, sort by ERR, and you have a ranked list of every channel in your niche with their contact buttons. The free tiers are enough for swap-hunting.
  • Swap chats and admin communities — Telegram search for "swap" in your language surfaces dozens of chats where admins post slots. Quality varies wildly; treat them as lead sources, verify every channel in TGStat before agreeing.
  • Adjacent-niche partners are the underrated move. Two channels for the same audience compete; two channels for neighboring audiences compound. A channel about productivity tools and one about remote jobs share a person but not a subject.

Writing the promo post: a teardown

Compare two swap posts for a fictional jobs channel:

Weak: "Great channel about jobs! Subscribe: @link" — no reason to care, no promise, and the reader has to leave the feed to learn anything.

Strong: "Every weekday at 9:00 — 5 remote design jobs with salaries listed, filtered from 200+ sources. Yesterday's batch had a 90k studio role. @link" — a promise with a rhythm, proof of filter quality, and a concrete example.

The structural rules visible in the teardown:

  • The first line must work as a notification. Most readers see only the preview.
  • One proof point beats three adjectives. "Yesterday's batch had a 90k role" is verifiable; "best jobs channel" is not.
  • End on the link, once. Multiple links split attention and trip spam filters in some clients.

extrasec_telegram-niche-research.content:
The engagement-rate math, with real thresholds

Niche research ultimately reduces to one calculation, and it's worth doing properly. ERR (engagement rate per post) = average views of the last 10 posts ÷ subscribers. TGStat and Telemetr both display it; the thresholds that matter:

  • Under 5% at any size: dead or inflated audience. If the niche's leaders all sit here, the niche's audience was bought, not built — a red flag for the whole category.
  • 5–15% for 10k+ channels: normal, healthy media territory.
  • 15–40% for channels under 5k: the sweet spot proving an audience actually reads. This is what a genuine gap looks like on a chart.
  • Over 60% on a big channel: verify before you celebrate — screenshot-farming and view-pods exist. Cross-check comments-to-views; real channels have both in proportion.

The research routine: list twenty candidate channels in the niche, pull ERR and growth slope for each, then read the top three by ERR for an hour. You'll leave knowing the working cadence, the formats that earn forwards, and — the actual prize — the gap between what audiences engage with and what anyone is providing.

Validation before commitment: the 10-question checklist

Before writing a single post, the niche should survive ten questions. The first five are about the audience:

  1. Can I name three specific people (not personas) who need this daily?
  2. Do they already gather somewhere I can observe?
  3. What do they currently read instead — and what does it miss?
  4. Would they notice if this channel vanished tomorrow? Why?
  5. Is the need recurring (daily/weekly) or one-time? One-time needs build launch spikes, not channels.

The second five are about you:

  1. Can I produce this from material I already read anyway?
  2. Does my format survive my worst week of the year?
  3. Am I one month from burnout on this topic, or one year?
  4. What's my unfair advantage — access, taste, data, speed?
  5. Would I run this if it never passed 500 subscribers?

Questions 7 and 10 kill more channels than any competitor. A niche that passes all ten is rare — that's the point. Most fail on 3 and 8, which means the fix is a narrower niche, not more willpower.

extrasec_telegram-post-formatting-guide.content:
The anatomy of a high-retention post

Formatting decisions compound differently at each layer of a post. A teardown of the structure that consistently performs:

  • Line one (the notification). Telegram truncates previews aggressively; the first ~60 characters decide whether the post opens at all. Front-load the specifics: a number, a name, a claim. "Ticket prices to Georgia dropped 40%" beats "Great news for travelers" every measurable way.
  • Paragraph rhythm. One to three sentences per paragraph, blank line between. Mobile screens fit roughly five lines; walls of text get skimmed into nothing. If a paragraph wraps more than a phone screen, it's two paragraphs.
  • Bold as navigation, not decoration. Bold the phrase a skimmer needs to find the post's spine — usually one bold phrase per paragraph. Bold whole sentences and nothing stands out; bold nothing and skimmers leave.
  • The single-link rule. Each post carries one action. Two links halve clicks on each; three turn the post into a directory nobody finishes.

Media captions: the limit nobody plans for

Captions have their own rules, and they're stricter than post text: 1,024 characters for a photo caption, 2,048 for some media types, and — the trap — no formatting entities survive in captions forwarded from some sources, plus albums show the caption only on the first item. Practical consequences:

  • If a post's text exceeds the caption limit, the pattern is: short caption on the media, full text as the next standalone post. Some channels put "1/2" markers; cleaner is the album-then-text pair sent as a scheduled sequence.
  • Album captions belong on the first image — plan which image leads, because it carries the entire caption.
  • Link previews and media don't mix: a post with a photo suppresses the link preview unless you strip the media. When the preview matters more than your own image, post text-only with the preview.

The post skeleton, line by line

The anatomy of a post that gets read to the end is stable enough to template. Line one — the promise: what the reader gets, concretely, in under 70 characters — this is also the preview text, so it must work alone. Line two — the turn: why now, or why you — one sentence of context that earns the read ("after three channels asked us the same question..."). The body — one idea per paragraph, bolded anchors: bold is the skimmer's map; three to five anchors per screen, each readable as a summary on its own. The artifact: screenshot, list or code block — the thing that survives being screenshotted out of context. The close: one call to action, never two (a post asking for a reaction, a comment and a click gets none). Save this as a draft template in your scheduler once, and every future post starts at 70% done — formatting discipline you don't have to re-decide daily.

The A/B habit: formatting as a testable variable

Formatting claims deserve the same skepticism as timing claims, and the test is cheap. Pick one variable per week — emoji section markers on/off, bold density high/low, quote blocks vs dashes, caption above vs below media — and alternate across comparable posts for two weeks. Compare 48-hour views and forwards per format pair; keep the winner, log it, and move to the next variable. Three disciplines make the results real: comparable content (a test between a giveaway post and an essay measures nothing), one variable at a time, and a fixed judgment horizon. Ten weeks of this produces something better than any style guide: a formatting manual derived from your audience's actual behavior — and the habit of testing, which outlives every specific finding.

extrasec_telegram-content-calendar.content:
A worked example: one month of a real calendar

Abstract calendars don't survive contact with a real channel, so here's a month for a (fictional but typical) 3-post-week design newsletter, built in one evening:

  • Slot structure: Monday = one tool deep-dive; Wednesday = three links worth your time, one line each; Friday = one teardown of a real design decision.
  • Batch 1 (45 min): list the month's four Monday tools — already known, they're what you used this month. Draft two-line stubs for each.
  • Batch 2 (60 min): expand each stub into a full post. Writing four similar posts consecutively is twice as fast as writing them across four weeks — no context re-loading.
  • Batch 3 (30 min): Wednesday link posts are just the reading list you already have open; Friday teardowns get drafted from notes you made anyway.
  • Queue (15 min): paste the date/message pairs into the scheduler — with a batching tool this is one message; with per-post bots, twelve. Done for a month.

Total: about 2.5 hours for 12 posts, once a month. The daily alternative costs roughly the same time spread across 12 switching-costs — and dies the first busy week.

The capture pipeline: where posts come from

The calendar answers when; the capture pipeline answers what. Channels that batch successfully all have some version of this:

  • One inbox, zero judgment. A saved-messages folder (or a private bot chat) where every candidate lands — links, screenshots, half-thoughts. The only rule: capture takes under five seconds or it doesn't happen.
  • Weekly triage against slots. Fifteen minutes: drag candidates onto the calendar's slots. What fills the slot gets written; what doesn't fit any slot gets deleted without guilt — the slot structure is the filter.
  • Draft in the format of the slot. Monday digests always look the same, which means drafting is filling a template, not composing from scratch.

The measurable payoff: a working capture pipeline means batching day contains zero blank-page moments. Everything is pre-decided; you're only editing.

extrasec_telegram-series-and-serialized-.content:
A real series plan: seven days, one case study

Here's a complete series arc that works for almost any niche — a week-long teardown, one post per day, ~150 words each:

  • Day 1 — The setup: the subject, the stakes, what will be examined. End with the question the week answers. Pin it; every later post links back implicitly by carrying the series title.
  • Days 2–5 — One facet per day: each post examines one layer (for a channel teardown: positioning, content mix, promotion, monetization), always with one concrete observation a stranger could learn from.
  • Day 6 — The synthesis: what the pieces add up to. This post earns the forwards; make it self-contained so it travels alone.
  • Day 7 — The archive: all seven posts as one long post. Newcomers arrive from the forwards into a finished artifact instead of a puzzle.

Scheduling note: draft all seven before day 1 goes out, then queue them. A daily series with a missing day breaks the appointment it exists to build.

The hashtag index: making a series navigable

A series without an index punishes every late joiner and caps how far the series can travel. The fix is three artifacts, all cheap. Tag every part: #buildlog 4/12 in the footer makes the whole series one tap away (tapping a hashtag searches the channel for it) and gives readers a progress marker. Pin or link an index post: one message listing all parts with links, updated as the series grows — this is what forwarders share. Open each part with a one-line recap: "Last time: we shipped the parser; today it breaks in production." New readers buy in at part five if the on-ramp costs ten seconds; without these artifacts they don't, and a reader who can't catch up silently waits for the series to end.

Pacing mechanics: the cliff, the gap and the payoff

Serialized retention is an engineering problem with known parts. Part length: 300–600 words per part is the sweet spot — long enough to deliver, short enough that "I'll read the next one" never becomes a chore. The cliff: end on an open loop the reader can feel — an unresolved number, a decision pending, a failure just discovered — not on a summary (summaries close loops, and closed loops don't bring anyone back). The gap: one day between parts builds the check-the-channel habit; a week between parts loses most casual readers mid-series, so for weekly cadence, make each part self-contained. The payoff rule: never stretch the finale — readers forgive a short series, never a padded one. Schedule the whole series in one sitting, gaps included, so pacing is a decision you made once instead of a mood you had each morning.

After the finale: the series as an asset

A finished series is an asset, and most channels abandon it the day it ends. The harvest routine: publish a finale index — the full list with links, framed as "the whole story in one place" — and pin it for a week; it consistently becomes one of the channel's most-forwarded posts because it's the format forwarders prefer. Then package: the same parts, lightly edited, become a PDF, a Notion page or the free artifact that anchors a paid tier — serialized content is pre-validated long-form, and bundling it costs an evening. Finally rerun: three months later, re-promote one part per week with a "from the archive" line. On channels that do this, archive reruns routinely pull view rates close to the original run — because half your current subscribers weren't there when it first ran.

extrasec_telegram-source-curation.content:
Attribution: the currency curators forget

Curated digests live on other people's material, and how you credit it is a strategic choice, not a courtesy. The practice that compounds:

  • Link the original source, always. Yes, it's an outbound link — and source channels notice referral traffic. Mid-size sources check their analytics and will mention or swap with curators who send readers.
  • Name the finder when you didn't find it. "(spotted in @channel)" costs eight characters and earns a peer who'll feed you stories later. Curation is a network disguised as a channel.
  • Add the take, carry the risk. Your one-line read on each item is the only part that's yours — and the only part that can be wrong in public. That's fine: curators with a visible stance build audiences; neutral reposters build nothing.

The intake stack, concretely

A working curator's intake has four parts. 1) An RSS reader (Feedly, Inoreader) holding 60–120 feeds — including your competitor digests, because you want to read what they read plus what they miss. 2) A dedicated Telegram folder with 30–50 source channels you never forward from without checking the original. 3) A capture chat: forward anything promising to a private "inbox" chat in one tap. 4) A weekly sweep of Hacker News and the relevant subreddits for the long tail. The inbox chat is your product backlog. If capture takes more than one tap, you'll stop by week three — curation dies of friction, not of laziness.

The 5-3-1 daily cut

From a full day of intake, publish the cut: 5 links that survive the question "would my reader act on this today?", 3 one-line takes on things you're not linking formally, 1 deep item — a teardown, a comparison, a larger curation. The volume discipline is the product: digests that fire off fifteen links a day train readers to skim; five links with context train readers to open. Readers feel the filter before they can articulate it, and your unsubscribe rate tracks every time you break the cut. When a slow news day tempts you to pad — don't. A digest that sometimes publishes less is trusted; a digest that always publishes something is ignored.

Speed vs correctness — pick a lane, label it

Every curator faces the dilemma: be twenty minutes early with a rumor or three hours late with a verified story. The solution is formats, not agonizing. Run a "fast lane" post type explicitly labeled unconfirmed, and a "verified" format that only carries checked material — readers forgive labeled speed, never unlabeled wrongness. And make corrections a feature, not an embarrassment: when you get something wrong, post the correction in a fixed format the same day. Curators who visibly correct are trusted; curators who never correct are assumed to never check. That assumption is the only thing in curation you can't rebuild after losing it.

extrasec_telegram-rss-bots.content:
A real RSS setup, component by component

A production RSS pipeline for a channel has four parts; here's the reference setup and the reasoning behind each:

  • The bridge. A FeedBridge-style bot or a self-hosted RSS-to-Telegram instance. Self-hosting wins at volume (no per-feed limits, your own filtering logic); a hosted bot wins for one feed and ten minutes of effort.
  • Keyword filters at the bridge. For broad sources, filter at intake with include/exclude keywords — every filtered item is a post you never have to unsee. Filter early, curate late.
  • A staging chat. Route the feed into a private chat, not the channel. This is the single highest-leverage setting: the feed becomes a staging queue a human promotes from, instead of a firehose a human apologizes for.
  • A digesting rhythm. A busy feed needs collapsing — the top five items of the day beat fifty instant posts. Some bridges support digest mode natively; otherwise the staging chat makes manual digesting trivial.

One maintenance rule: review the source list quarterly. Feeds die quietly, and a pipeline that stops updating is worse than none — it hides the silence.

Filters and templates: making the feed yours

The difference between an RSS bot that helps and one that floods is the two configuration layers most people skip. Filters: per-feed keyword rules — only post entries matching "russia*-related terms" or your product names, block anything tagged "sponsored" — cut a firehose to a stream; the global block list (competitor names, words that always mean noise in your niche) does the rest. Templates: per-feed post formatting — a title line, a one-sentence rule, the link, and a hashtag for the source — turns machine output into something that reads like your channel. Budget the regex-level effort for an evening, not an afternoon: feeds drift, and a filter list reviewed quarterly catches the source that quietly changed its RSS structure and started posting raw HTML. The bot's job is plumbing; the curation still has to be yours.

The hybrid feed: automation with a human gate

For channels where voice matters more than speed, the setup that works is RSS-to-review, not RSS-to-publish: the bot posts new feed items into a private editor's chat instead of the channel, and a human promotes the ones worth publishing — one tap to forward into the scheduler's draft flow, two taps to publish immediately. You keep the machine's completeness (nothing is ever missed) while the channel keeps its voice (nothing is published unread). The cost is honest: five to fifteen minutes a day at realistic feed volumes, which is exactly the job a curation channel claims to do manually anyway. Channels that outgrow the hybrid usually demote it in a predictable order: news they always publish goes fully automated, analysis stays human, and the review chat shrinks to a checklist — automation earning its autonomy one verified pattern at a time.

When RSS is the wrong tool

Some sources don't fit the pipe, and forcing them creates worse output than manual posting. JS-heavy sites with no real feed publish summaries so stripped the bot posts ellipses — those sources deserve a manual slot or a different bridge. Paywalled outlets export headline-plus-paywall links, which reads as teasing content you can't deliver. Social feeds (Twitter/X, YouTube channels) have unstable or rate-limited bridges that break silently; for YouTube specifically, channels and playlists usually work better through dedicated notification bots than generic RSS. And sources that matter in minutes — breaking news, price alerts — are a polling-frequency problem RSS bots handle poorly. The mature stack admits the gap: RSS for the steady 80%, manual or specialized tools for the moments where speed or context is the product.

extrasec_telegram-moderation-bots.content:
A worked anti-spam configuration

Concrete starting settings that keep a discussion group of a few thousand members clean without punishing regulars:

  • Shieldy: captcha on, but only during waves (it has an on/off toggle — leave it off in calm periods); delete messages with links from accounts younger than 24 hours; limit join-and-post to one message in the first minute.
  • Rose: warn-then-mute ladder (2 warnings → 1h mute → 1 day → ban); blacklist the obvious crypto/pharma patterns rather than individual words; lock stickers-and-gifs in the channel-adjacent announcements group if you run one.
  • Combot: run its reports weekly — the useful signal isn't the spam it caught but the activity distribution: a group where 5 people produce 90% of messages is a group about to go quiet, and the fix is content prompts, not moderation.

The whitelist discipline that ties it together: your own channel, admin accounts, and the bots themselves get whitelisted first. Half of all "the bot is broken" reports are the bot moderating another bot.

Rose: the 20-minute configuration that matters

The practical Rose setup for a discussion group: /settings → captcha on (button, 120-second timeout) to catch the join-and-spam wave; locks set to links=admins-only and forwards=off during spam waves; warns at three, with the action set to a 24-hour mute; media restrictions on voice notes and video notes if the group is a discussion annex and not a hangout. The rule of thumb for every lock: you're trading false positives for spam friction. Start permissive, tighten after incidents, never pre-tighten "to be safe" — over-locked groups moderate ghosts while the real spam adapts faster than your lock list.

Shieldy's philosophy — and when it backfires

Shieldy is aggressive by design: it deletes messages from brand-new members that contain links or forwards, throws a CAPTCHA at joins, and it does this with almost no configuration. That default profile is perfect for public channels with linked groups that catch spam waves right after every promo post. It's wrong for communities whose members legitimately share links — a dev group posting repos or a deals group posting shops will get eaten alive by Shieldy's freshness rules. The honest test: if more than one real member per week loses a message to the bot, the group has outgrown Shieldy's defaults — move to Rose warns with a human-reviewable ladder, and keep Shieldy in reserve for the next attack wave.

Combot: moderation as data

Combot's real value isn't its captcha — it's the per-user history. Three uses that change decisions: spot sleepers (accounts that joined weeks ago, said nothing, and activate the day your promo goes out); check a loud critic's history before banning — a two-year member with three thousand messages is not a wave account; and lean on the global spam database, which flags known scammer accounts at join time. Pair it with the weekly top-members digest: your most active participants are your future moderators, and promoting from the data instead of from who shouts loudest is how groups stay healthy as they grow.

The escalation ladder every group needs

Write the ladder down before you need it: 1) automatic — captcha and obvious spam deleted by the bots; 2) /warn — three warnings trigger an automatic 24-hour mute; 3) /mute 1h for heated violations that shouldn't count as formal warnings; 4) /ban reserved for scams, rings and doxxing; 5) always state the reason, publicly, in one line. Pin the ladder as a single message. Groups die from moderator mood swings more often than from spam — a published, predictable ladder makes enforcement boring, and boring enforcement is what members read as fairness. When someone complains about a mute, you answer with the pinned message, not with your mood.

extrasec_telegram-scheduler-comparison.content:
The cost structure nobody compares

Feature tables miss the economics. What scheduling actually costs on each path, over a year of real use:

  • Native composer: free in money, expensive in switching — one post at a time means opening the app daily, forever. At 15+ posts a month the calendar tax becomes real hours.
  • Free bots (ManyBot class): free in money and mostly in time; the cost is ceilings — media size limits, menu-driven flows that slow bulk entry, and support that's a community chat.
  • Premium schedulers: a few dollars a month, and the honest math is against your hourly rate: if batching saves two hours monthly, the tool pays for itself in the first queue.
  • Self-hosted: a VPS (a few dollars a month), your time to build and maintain, and total control. The comparison that matters is against the hours you'd spend debugging it — treat it as a hobby with a deliverable.

The line that decides: under ~10 posts a week, native is genuinely fine. Beyond that, every path's cost is really a question of how much a lost publishing day costs your channel.

The native composer: what it does and where it stops

Telegram's built-in scheduling deserves its due before any tool comparison: it's free, offline-proof, and the scheduled post is editable up to the moment it sends — for a one-off post tomorrow at nine, nothing beats it. Where it stops is a short list that defines every scheduler's pitch. No queue overview: the composer shows one scheduled post per open chat, not a calendar of what's coming — planning a week means scrolling. No drafts library: reusable templates, pillar skeletons and evergreen posts live in your notes app, not in the tool. No cross-channel view: two channels means two composers and a memory. No analytics: scheduling natively means stats come from somewhere else. If you publish twice a week, the native scheduler is the right tool; the moment the question "what's queued for Thursday?" appears, a tool with a queue earns its keep.

Migrating between schedulers without double-posting

Switching tools has one classic disaster — the old scheduler and the new one both fire the same post. The safe migration order: freeze (stop adding to the old queue a week before the switch), export (copy pending drafts out — most tools at least show scheduled posts; a screenshots-plus-notes export is undignified but complete), revoke (remove the old tool's admin rights and, for token-based tools, reissue the token — a live token in an abandoned tool is a safety issue, not a tidiness one), rebuild the queue in the new tool from the exported plan, and overlap for one week with the old tool idle before deleting anything. The one-week overlap is the insurance: queues don't always export, tokens don't always transfer, and discovering either on day one of a fresh tool is how gaps happen. Migrations done this way are boring, which is the goal.

The small print that decides daily happiness

The comparison tables miss the details that decide whether a scheduler becomes part of your hands. Timezone honesty: the tool must show your audience's local time or a fixed home zone — "9:00" in whose morning? Daylight-saving drift has silently moved more channels' schedules than any hack. Silent send: a toggle per post, not a global setting — night posts to other timezones shouldn't ring phones. Preview fidelity: you need to see the post as subscribers will — media order, caption truncation, link preview — because the preview is the last QA gate. Edit-after-schedule: real life edits posts after they're queued; tools that force delete-and-resend lose small fixes. Draft storage: where do your pillar templates live? Inside the tool beats a notes app by a mile. Test these five in the free tier before comparing price — they're the difference between a tool you open daily and one you abandon by February.

What to automate first: a 30-day graduation path

For owners drowning in manual publishing, the order of adoption matters more than the tool choice. Week one: move scheduled publishing itself — all posts enter a queue, nothing is posted live by hand except true announcements. This single change captures most of the stress reduction, because the failure mode it removes ("I forgot to post today") is the one that damages rhythm most. Week two: build the drafts library — pillar templates and three evergreen posts stored in the tool, so empty slots have a fallback. Week three: add the media checks — albums prebuilt and previewed in the queue, not assembled at publish time. Week four: add the review loop — a weekly look at what published, what flopped, what's queued. A month in, the channel runs on rails with the human doing only two things: writing and deciding. Tools that promise to remove those two are removing the channel.

extrasec_telegram-bot-commands-cheatshee.content:
Building your own cheatsheet: the method

Any printed cheatsheet decays; the sustainable version is a personal one, built in an hour and maintained in minutes. The method:

  • A pinned message per tool. One pinned post in your own saved messages or a private "ops" channel per tool you run — BotFather, your scheduler, Combot, Rose. Ten commands each, the ones you actually type.
  • Copy from history, not memory. Scroll your own chat history with each bot and write down what you really used in the last month. The commands you think you use and the ones you actually use differ more than anyone expects.
  • Record the failure commands too. The error message you always forget (date format, ID format) belongs on the sheet — that's the one you look up under time pressure.
  • Review quarterly. Delete what you stopped using. A cheatsheet with thirty lines lies to you; one with twelve works.

Designing your own command set (for bots you build)

Once a channel runs a custom bot — a tip line, a member tracker, an internal tool — the command surface is worth designing like a product. Three rules from bots that aged well.
